Among 147 clinicians participating in a post-intervention survey, 4 (3%) selected one or 2, 12 (8%) selected 3, and 131 (89%) selected four or 5 on a 5-point Likert scale rating their confidence (1, less confident; 5, more confident) in not prescribing antibiotics after SPOTFIRE results.
DISCUSSION

In this study, we used an implementation science approach to evaluate the effect of POC multiplex testing combined with an antibiotic stewardship program on antibiotic prescribing practices. We observed a significant reduction in antibiotic prescriptions after this intervention.

The MITIGATE toolkit provides a step-by-step evidence-based implementation guide for ED and urgent care settings and has been successfully adapted to ambulatory care and urgent care clinics. However, to our knowledge, the current study is the first to demonstrate the utility of implementing MITIGATE in the context of multiplex POC testing for respiratory pathogen testing.

Implementation of antibiotic stewardship interventions for ARIs in ED and urgent care settings is feasible and effective. In prior work, we found that intensive behavioral nudging methods did not impact prescribing behavior in academic settings, possibly because antibiotic-inappropriate prescribing was already uncommon given the lower prescribing rates in these settings, perhaps due to the presence of trainees and evidence-based practices. However, implementation of these programs in a large rural healthcare system with high antibiotic prescribing rates resulted in a significant reduction in inappropriate prescribing for ARIs.

Our findings align with those of prior work demonstrating the potential role of POC testing in mitigating inappropriate antibiotic use, ultimately contributing to improved antimicrobial stewardship. Cohen et al. reported a 36% reduction in antibiotic prescriptions for pharyngitis after the implementation of rapid streptococcal antigen testing in urgent care settings. Zhang et al. reported a 24% decrease in antibiotic use when C-reactive protein testing was employed to guide treatment decisions for lower respiratory tract infections. In a meta-analysis, multiplex testing reduced time to results, improved antiviral use, and reduced ED and hospital length of stay.

Despite its advantages, integrating POC testing into routine clinical practice presents several challenges. Antimicrobial prescribing is a complex behavior that is influenced by a combination of factors. Aside from individual provider characteristics (e.g., knowledge, skills, memory, attention, and decision-making), there are external influences (e.g., peer comparison) that differ by context and setting. Financial constraints, including the cost of POC devices and reimbursement issues, remain significant barriers. Additionally, clinician adherence and confidence in POC-guided decision-making can vary, with some providers expressing concerns about test accuracy and reliability, although PCR-based POC testing is highly accurate. Moreover, POC testing is not universally available, with rural and low-resource settings having limited availability despite their high burden of infectious diseases. Addressing these challenges requires targeted educational initiatives, policy support, and infrastructure investment to maximize the benefits of POC testing in antimicrobial stewardship.
Limitations

Our study had limitations. All enrollment occurred at a single center in a high-prescribing area during the nonrespiratory season, and our control group was based on retrospective data obtained from the EHR. Future study with a concurrent control group (e.g., randomized controlled trial), multisite study, or longer cohort may be warranted. Clinicians and patients in the prospective arm of our study could opt out of participating, which could have biased our results. Self-reported data obtained in patient interviews were subject to recall bias and could have impacted our results. Our study is also at risk of the Hawthorne effect as providers could not be blinded to the intervention.
Conclusion

Combining POC testing with an antimicrobial stewardship intervention resulted in reduced antibiotic prescribing in an urgent care setting. Implementation of POC testing could enhance ongoing efforts to encourage appropriate prescribing practices through clinical education, guideline implementation, and stewardship programs.

passages.text: Treatment outcomes of sunitinib and/or pazopanib in advanced alveolar soft part sarcoma: A Turkish Oncology Group (TOG) study

Alveolar soft part sarcoma (ASPS) is an ultra-rare, highly angiogenic sarcoma with limited responsiveness to chemotherapy. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) such as sunitinib and pazopanib have shown promising activity, but comparative real-world data remain scarce. This multicenter, retrospective study included 51 patients with metastatic ASPS treated with sunitinib and/or pazopanib between January 2013 and March 2025. Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier methods, and prognostic factors were assessed via Cox regression. First-line TKI therapy achieved significantly longer median PFS compared with chemotherapy (24.9 vs. 5.8 months; p < 0.001), without a significant OS difference. In first-line comparisons, pazopanib demonstrated a trend toward longer PFS (27.2 vs. 15.2 months; p = 0.052) and significantly prolonged OS (45.0 vs. 21.0 months; p = 0.021) versus sunitinib. Across all lines, median PFS and OS were 24.9 and 38.3 months for pazopanib, and 17.7 and 21.0 months for sunitinib, respectively. Multivariate analysis identified prior chemotherapy and liver metastases as independent predictors of shorter PFS. Both agents were well tolerated, with mostly Grade 1-2 toxicities. In one of the largest real-world ASPS cohorts, frontline TKIs provided substantial disease control and prolonged survival compared with chemotherapy, with manageable toxicity. These findings reinforce the role of anti-angiogenic therapy as a preferred first-line approach in advanced ASPS. Prospective studies are warranted to optimize treatment sequencing in this ultra-rare sarcoma.

passages.text: Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1038/s41598-025-29276-9.
Introduction

Alveolar soft part sarcoma (ASPS) is an extremely rare type of soft tissue sarcoma accounting for < 1% of all sarcomas. It predominantly affects adolescents and young adults . It is characterized by an indolent course; however, it has a high tendency to metastasize even in the presence of a relatively slow-growing primary tumor . Over half of patients present with distant metastases, most commonly to the lungs (around 90% of cases). The rate of brain metastasis (10-20%) is notably higher in ASPS than in other sarcomas . Surgical resection of primary lesion and oligometastases remains the mainstay for long-term control when it is feasible . The prognosis in advanced or metastatic cases remains poor, with 5-year OS rates under 20% in historical series. Conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy has minimal efficacy in this disease, with objective response rates of less than 10% and poor progression-free survival(PFS) .

The rarity of ASPS and its chemoresistance pose major therapeutic challenges. There is currently no consensus on the optimal systemic treatment for advanced or metastatic ASPS. However, novel systemic therapies are critically needed for unresectable metastatic ASPS. Molecular insights have provided a rationale for targeted approaches.

In recent years, growing evidence suggests that ASPS is a highly angiogenic tumor- driven by a characteristic unbalanced TFE3 fusion that upregulates pro-angiogenic pathways - which provides a rationale for anti-angiogenic therapies . Multi-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) with anti-angiogenic activity have shown notable activity in this disease, significantly improving clinical outcomes compared to chemotherapy . Immunotherapy has recently become an important treatment option in alveolar soft part sarcoma (ASPS). The anti-PD-L1 antibody atezolizumab has shown meaningful clinical activity, with objective responses observed in patients with advanced or metastatic ASPS in phase II trials . Based on these results, atezolizumab has been currently recommended as a first-line treatment option for unresectable or metastatic ASPS.

Sunitinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor with direct antitumour and antiangiogenic activity targeting platelet-derived growth factor receptors (PDGFR), vascular endothelial growth factor receptors (VEGFR) and RET, was one of the first agents to demonstrate promising activity against ASPS . In a retrospective series, sunitinib demonstrated prolonged progression-free and overall survival in patients with ASPS .

Pazopanib, a multi-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor with activity against VEGFR, PDGFR, and KIT, has also been used in the treatment of ASPS . While the PALETTE trial demonstrated a clinical benefit in advanced soft tissue sarcomas, it included only a limited number of ASPS patients . More meaningful insights come from real-world studies, which suggest that pazopanib offers clinical benefit in later treatment lines . Retrospective comparisons have also indicated superior disease control and survival outcomes with pazopanib compared to trabectedin in ASPS .

Given the scarcity of prospective studies in this ultra-rare sarcoma, retrospective analyses play a crucial role in expanding our understanding of treatment outcomes. The present multi-center retrospective study was undertaken to evaluate the clinical outcomes of patients with advanced ASPS treated with sunitinib and/or pazopanib.
Materials and methods
Study design and patient selection

This multicenter, retrospective study included patients diagnosed with metastatic ASPS who were treated with sunitinib and/or pazopanib from January 2013 to March 2025. This study included data from 17 oncology centers across Turkey. Eligible patients were identified through institutional medical records. Inclusion criteria comprised histologically confirmed ASPS, patients who were diagnosed with metastatic disease at presentation or who developed metastases during the disease course, and administration of sunitinib and/or pazopanib during the treatment course. Patients with insufficient data on clinical course or treatment outcomes were excluded from the analysis. Demographic features, ECOG performance status, comorbidities, tumor localization, stage at diagnosis, and sites of metastasis (lung, bone, liver, and brain) were collected. Treatment-related adverse events were recorded according to CTCAE version 5.0.
Outcomes

PFS was defined as the interval between the initiation of TKI (sunitinib and/or pazopanib) or chemotherapy and either radiographic or clinical disease progression or death from any cause or last follow-up. OS was defined as the time from TKI (sunitinib and/or pazopanib) or chemotherapy initiation to death from any cause or last follow-up. Survival status and treatment responses were confirmed through hospital records.
Statistical analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize patient demographics and clinical characteristics. Categorical variables were reported as frequencies and percentages. Median PFS and OS were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and Kaplan-Meier curves were used to estimate survival across treatment subgroups. Depending on the hypothesized timing of group differences, either the log-rank test (for proportional hazard assumptions and evenly distributed events) or the Breslow (generalized Wilcoxon) test (for early event predominance) was applied to compare survival distributions.

Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with PFS. Variables with p < 0.20 in univariate analysis were included in the multivariate model. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported.

All statistical analyses were conducted using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences, version 26.0 (SPSS Inc, Chicago, IL), and a two-sided p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results

A total of 51 patients with histologically confirmed ASPS were included. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics are presented in Table 1. The median age was 35 years; 52.9% were female, and 76.5% had an ECOG performance status of 0. Lung metastasis was observed in 84.3% of patients, bone metastasis in 25.5%, and brain metastasis in 23.5%. First-line metastatic treatment consisted of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) in 56.9% of cases and chemotherapy in 43.1%.

Treatment outcomes: TKI vs. chemotherapy

Patients treated with TKIs had a significantly longer PFS compared to those receiving chemotherapy in the first-line (median PFS: 24.9 months [16.8-33.0, 95% CI] vs. 5.8 months [2.0-9.6, 95% CI]; p < 0.001; Fig. 1A). However, the difference in OS between the two groups was not statistically significant (median OS: 30.9 months [19.9-42.8, 95% CI] for TKI vs. 47.8 months [27.9-67.7, 95% CI] for chemotherapy; p = 0.086; Fig. 2A).

Multivariate Cox regression identified chemotherapy use (vs. TKI) as an independent predictor of poor PFS (HR: 9.52, 95% CI: 3.7-24.3; p < 0.001), along with the presence of liver metastasis (HR: 4.12, 95% CI: 1.2-14.1; p = 0.024) (Table 2).

Comparison of Sunitinib and pazopanib

When all the treatment lines were evaluated together, 30 patients received sunitinib; 36 patients pazopanib, and 15 patients both pazopanib and sunitinib in different treatment lines. When those 30 patients receiving sunitinib were evaluated separately, mPFS was 17.7 months and mOS was 21.0 months, regardless of the treatment line. Among 36 patients who received pazopanib, mPFS was 24.9 months and mOS was 38.3 months.

In the first-line treatment, 15 patients received sunitinib and 14 patients received pazopanib. Median PFS was numerically longer in the pazopanib group compared to sunitinib in the first-line (15.2 months [13.2-17.1, 95% CI] vs. 27.2 months [23.7-30.7, 95% CI]; p = 0.052; Fig. 1B). A statistical significance was observed for OS, favoring pazopanib over sunitinib (45.0 months vs. 21.0 months; p = 0.021; Fig. 2B).

Detailed time-point survival probabilities are summarized in Table 3. At 12 months, PFS rates were 66% for pazopanib and 63% for sunitinib; at 24 months, these rates were 50% vs. 35%, respectively. Similarly, OS rates at 12 months were 76% vs. 83%; at 36 months OS was 59% and 28%, respectively.

Effect of treatment line

When stratified by line of therapy, sunitinib showed no significant difference in either PFS (15.2 [13.2-17.1, 95%CI] vs. 18.2 [3.2-32.8, 95%CI] months; p = 0.422; Fig. 1C) or OS (21.0 [14.1-28.0, 95%CI] vs. 20.1 [3.5-38.6, 95%CI] months; p = 0.819; Fig. 2C) between first-line and later-line use.

In contrast, pazopanib demonstrated a significantly prolonged PFS when used as a first-line treatment (27.2 months [23.7-30.7, 95%CI]) compared to second-line or beyond (10.2 months [3.3-17.1, 95%CI]; p = 0.020; Fig. 1D) and OS (p = 0.021; Fig. 2D).

Among patients who received first-line chemotherapy, the mPFS of sunitinib in the second line was 20.1 months (n = 11), whereas the mPFS of pazopanib was 31.9 months (n = 8) (p:0.142). In these 19 patients, the mPFS was 24.1 months.

In the chemotherapy-first group, 19 of 22 patients received a TKI as second-line therapy, whereas 3 patients were treated with another chemotherapeutic regimen. The treatment sequence summary and second-line efficacy data are presented in the Supplementary Material.
Safety profile

Adverse events associated with TKI therapy are summarized in Table 4. Both sunitinib and pazopanib were generally well tolerated. Grade 1-2 adverse events for sunitinib included anemia (36.7%), nausea (33.3%), and skin toxicity (30.0%). Grade 3-4 toxicities occurred in a minority of patients, mainly thrombocytopenia (3.3%), nausea (3.3%), stomatitis (3.3%), and skin toxicity (3.3%). For pazopanib, nausea (33.4%), anemia (27.8%), diarrhea (22.2%), and hypothyroidism (22.2%) were among the most frequently observed grade 1-2 toxicities. Grade 3-4 toxicities were uncommon, with diarrhea (2.8%), hypothyroidism (2.8%). Dose reduction was required in four patients (13.3%) receiving sunitinib and in one patient (2.8%) treated with pazopanib. No treatment discontinuations occurred due to adverse events.

Discussion

In this multicenter series of 51 patients, first-line TKI therapy produced a striking PFS advantage over chemotherapy. The median PFS for frontline sunitinib/pazopanib was 24.9 months versus just 5.8 months for chemotherapy (p < 0.001). We also found that pazopanib tended to outperform sunitinib when administered as the initial therapy. First-line pazopanib treatment resulted in a median PFS of 27.2 months, compared to 15.2 months for sunitinib (p = 0.052), and OS was also significantly longer at 45.0 months versus 21.0 months (p = 0.021). Regardless of treatment line, the mPFS for sunitinib was 17.7 months and the mOS was 21.0 months (n = 30). Pazopanib had an mPFS of 24.9 months and an mOS of 38.3 months (n = 36).

The ASPS outcomes reported in this analysis were substantially better than those in unselected STS trials. For example, the phase III PALETTE trial of mixed STS patients reported a mPFS of only 4.6 months on pazopanib . All patients included in the PALETTE study had received prior chemotherapy. In our study, the mPFS of patients who received second-line TKI after chemotherapy was 24.1 months, reflecting the particular sensitivity of ASPS to anti-angiogenic TKIs. This may be explained by the high vascularity structure of ASPS, several retrospective ASPS cohorts have suggested durable TKI efficacy. For example, Jagodzinska-Mucha et al. reported a median PFS of ~ 19 months with sunitinib, and Stacchiotti et al. observed a median PFS of 13.6 months with pazopanib . Our study exceeds these mPFSs, which likely reflects our use of TKIs in a front-line setting in 29 patients. It is now known that ASPS is a chemoresistant tumour, and these data support the use of TKI therapy at an earlier stage in the treatment of ASPS.

Notably, Fernandes et al. recently described a real-world ASPS cohort in which 24 metastatic patients received first-line TKIs and achieved a median PFS of 12 months. While 14 of the 24 patients in this study used sunitinib, the other 10 patients received different TKI treatments, including pazopanib, sorafenib, and crizotinib. The mPFS was 15 months in the sunitinib group and 11 months in the other TKI group. In our study, the mPFS of 15 patients who received sunitinib as first-line treatment was 15.2 months, similar to the study by Fernandes et al. .

We also found that pazopanib tended to outperform sunitinib when given as initial therapy: first-line pazopanib yielded a median PFS of 27.3 months versus 15.2 months for sunitinib (p = 0.052), and OS was significantly longer (45.0 vs. 21.1 months, p = 0.021). It is consistent with other reports showing that not all TKIs are equivalent in ASPS. For example, a Chinese retrospective found pazopanib PFS (13.7 mo) to be shorter than that of anlotinib (23.6 mo) in a second-line setting . Although our pazopanib PFS was unusually high, it may reflect better tolerability and sustained dosing of pazopanib, or simply the advantage of earlier line use. Importantly, in multivariate analysis, the only independent predictors of shorter PFS were prior chemotherapy use and the presence of liver metastases. The latter finding suggests that visceral liver spread, less common than pulmonary metastasis, may mark a more aggressive ASPS phenotype.

OS in our cohort did not significantly differ between upfront TKI versus chemotherapy (median ~ 31 vs. 48 months, p = 0.086), possibly because all patients used TKI after progression. Moreover, the numerically longer median OS observed in the chemotherapy group compared to the TKI group may be partly attributed to the longer follow-up duration among patients who received chemotherapy as first-line treatment (median 58.1 vs. 33.4 months, respectively). In addition, potential selection bias inherent to the retrospective study design should be considered, as patients selected for first-line chemotherapy might have had more favorable baseline characteristics or less aggressive disease biology, which could have influenced survival outcomes. However, the substantially longer OS with first-line pazopanib warrants further study.  Historical series have reported a median OS with sunitinib of around 56 months , whereas our sunitinib cohort had a median OS of only ~ 21 months, underscoring the variability inherent in small samples or short follow-up. In the study by Fernandes et al., the mOS of patients using pazopanib was 54.4 months, while in our study it was 45 months with first-line treatment. In aggregate, our results support that TKI therapy provides markedly superior disease control compared with conventional chemotherapy, consistent with the literature on ASPS and other vascular sarcomas.

The safety profile of both TKIs in our series was consistent with known toxicities . Most patients experienced mild-to-moderate events: common Grade 1-2 AEs included fatigue, nausea, anemia, diarrhea, and skin changes. Grade 3-4 events were relatively infrequent. In line with prior reports, we observed that pazopanib was particularly prone to hepatotoxicity: Westerdijk et al. reported liver toxicity in 19% of 133 patients receiving pazopanib for sarcoma or renal cancer . By contrast, sunitinib-associated hepatic injury was uncommon. Overall, no unexpected safety problems emerged. Given the substantial clinical benefit, the adverse events profile of these agents appears acceptable if carefully managed.

passages.text: Recent advances in immunotherapy have significantly changed the treatment landscape of ASPS. The anti-PD-L1 antibody atezolizumab has demonstrated durable clinical activity and is now approved as a first-line option for unresectable or metastatic ASPS . While tyrosine kinase inhibitors remain an established standard, the incorporation of immune checkpoint blockade represents an important step toward improving long-term outcomes. Future studies should clarify the optimal sequencing or combination of TKIs and immunotherapy in this rare disease.

This study's retrospective design and relatively small sample size impose important limitations. Another important limitation of this study was that the choice of initial therapy (TKI or chemotherapy) varied between centers and, some patients received two lines of TKI (both sunitinib and pazopanib) therapy. The major strength of this study is that, to our knowledge, this is one of the largest multi-center real-world cohorts of patients with advanced ASPS treated with TKIs. Given the rarity of this sarcoma subtype, our sample size of 51 patients provides a valuable contribution to the limited literature. Conducting prospective trials is challenging in such rare tumors.

In summary, our real-world data demonstrate that both sunitinib and pazopanib achieve high disease control rates and prolonged PFS/OS in ASPS patients. These outcomes are substantially better than in other STS subtypes and considerably superior to historical outcomes with chemotherapy. These findings are consistent with the emerging consensus from ASPS cohorts worldwide, emphasizing the critical role of anti-angiogenic therapy in this disease.

passages.text: Establishing consensus on the implementation of Anticoagulation Stewardship Program with cardiologists in Pakistan: A Delphi study
Background

The Anticoagulation Stewardship Program (ASP) improves clinical outcomes, promotes patient safety, and supports healthcare systems in delivering high-quality, evidence-based anticoagulation management. This study aimed to develop a consensus among cardiologists about the implementation of the ASP Program in Pakistan.
Methods

A three-round Delphi study was conducted utilizing an online questionnaire. In Round 1, cardiologists (Delphi panel experts) reported their consensus with the items in the questionnaire using a 3-point Likert scale. The selection of items for Round 2 was based on acceptance by >=66.6% of the cardiologists and the agreement of the scientific committee. In Round 2, the panelists assessed those items that failed to gain consensus in Round 1. In Round 3, a face-to-face meeting was conducted among the scientific committee to evaluate the items that failed to gain expert agreement in Round 2 to form the final consensus document. Descriptive statistics was used to present the data.
Results

A total of 90 cardiologists from 30 hospitals were invited to participate in the study. Of these, 75 agreed to participate in Round 1 of the study (83% response rate). 68 cardiologists completed the survey in Round 2. Initially, 33 items from four domains were evaluated by the Delphi experts in Round 1. 18 items reached consensus in Round 1, 4 items reached consensus in Round 2, and 2 items reached consensus in Round 3. The final consensus document comprised 24 items. The study showed absolute consensus among national cardiologists regarding the implementation of ASP in Pakistan. A considerable agreement was achieved regarding essential components needed to strengthen ASP for anticoagulation management in the cardiology departments.
Conclusion

This study emphasized the need for educational sessions for patients and healthcare professionals, collaboration with healthcare authorities, and allocation of financial resources for ASP. This study also identified consensus among cardiologists on the perceived benefits of ASP for patients and the healthcare system. Several barriers that hindered the implementation of ASP in Pakistan were identified, including patient- and healthcare system-related barriers.
Introduction

A large number of patients utilize anticoagulant therapy globally to manage cardiovascular diseases such as atrial fibrillation, coronary heart disease, congestive heart failure, heart attack, and venous thromboembolism. A meta-analysis of studies on anticoagulant use reported that there was increase in the use of oral anticoagulants from 2010 to 2018. Contemporaneously, there has additionally been a substantial increase in adverse drug events (ADEs) related to anticoagulants, including high-risk bleeding and thromboembolic complications. This necessitates the careful use of anticoagulants, considering the fact that prescribing practices and patient attributes such as age, co-morbidities, concomitant use of other medications, and pharmacogenetics highly influence the incidence of ADEs.

The notion of stewardship programs started in the late 20th century to promote judicious use of antimicrobials. The antimicrobial stewardship program remained very effective at reducing the occurrence of adverse drug reactions (ADRs), healthcare costs, antimicrobial resistance and improving clinical outcomes among patients. In 2014, the ADEs associated with anticoagulants surpassed antibiotics as a leading cause of emergency department visits in the United States (US). The US National Action Plan for ADE prevention (2014) also documented that anticoagulants were not only the leading cause of emergency department visits among outpatients but also caused ADEs in 10% of inpatients on anticoagulation therapy. Considering this, anticoagulants were included in the initial targets of the ADE action plan along with antidiabetics and opioids which eventually led to the foundation of the anticoagulation stewardship program (ASP). In 2019, the US Anticoagulation Forum published a guide on the essential elements of the ASP with the aim to promote effective use of anticoagulants across all healthcare institutions. One study each from the US and Canada further laid down the basis of pharmacist-led ASP through evidence of feasibility, acceptance by the prescribing physicians, and better patient outcomes. The ASP, which is referred to as an integrated, effective, and system- related measure to optimize anticoagulant use and prevent avoidable ADEs, was successfully implemented in the US with documented cost savings and better patient outcomes. Furthermore, various studies in the United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada also documented the positive impact of ASP on maintaining high standards of care and enhancing hospital medication safety protocols.

passages.text: The implementation of ASP in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), including Pakistan, encounters distinct challenges attributable to constraints in resources, discrepancies in healthcare infrastructure, and restricted access to specialized medical services. According to the 2019 Global Burden of Disease study, the estimated incidence of cardiovascular diseases in Pakistan was around 918 per 100,000 population, and the estimated mortality rate was around 358 per 100,000 population. Various studies reported that one-fifth of middle-aged adults in Pakistan were at risk of developing coronary artery disease, whereas overall cardiovascular diseases were responsible for around 27% of the total deaths. Despite the excessive use of anticoagulants and the risk of serious adverse effects, numerous studies from Pakistan revealed that there were no standard guidelines for anticoagulant management, and a holistic approach focusing on continuum of care, quality improvement, and addressing patient-, clinician-, and healthcare system-level barriers was missing. These gaps contributed to higher rates of anticoagulant-related complications, hospital readmissions, and unnecessary healthcare costs, all placing an additional burden on an already strained healthcare system in Pakistan. Implementation of ASP in Pakistani hospitals could address these challenges by establishing a standardized, evidence-based framework for the safe and effective use of anticoagulants.

We conducted the first Delphi study in Pakistan, which presented extensive consensus points specifically from cardiologists for implementing ASP in Pakistan. The Delphi approach is a credible agreement technique of collecting expert views, which includes a confidential stepwise procedure involving multiple rounds of feedback to achieve consensus among Delphi experts.
Methodology
Study design

This study was a countrywide, multicenter, three-round Delphi study to obtain expert views on implementing ASP in Pakistan. It was entirely centered on the responses given by the Delphi experts related to significant issues with the implementation of the ASP. The Delphi technique is a broadly recognized scientific process of organized and systematic knowledge gathering from a group of experts (i.e., a Delphi panel) on contentious or complicated issues using a series of questionnaires. All panel experts offer their insights independently and confidentially, thereby mitigating the potential influence of dominant personalities or collective pressure. The Delphi process concludes upon reaching a consensus regarding the topics under discussion. In this study, a modified Delphi method was employed, as outlined by the RAND Corporation and the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) recommendations. The Delphi process was conducted in a systematic manner comprising seven distinct phases: 1) Comprehensive literature review conducted by the scientific committee; 2) Generation of discussion topics and questionnaire items by the scientific committee during an in-person meeting; 3) Selection of an expert panel for the Delphi process; 4) Invitation extended to potential participants to take part in the Delphi process; 5) Evaluation of the domain and item set by the expert panel through two iterative rounds utilizing an online platform, adhering to a two-round Delphi methodology; 6) Final deliberation among the experts regarding items that did not gain the expert consensus in the previous rounds; 7) Final consensus analysis (Fig 1).
Delphi steps.

Data were collected between June and December 2023, and the ethical approval was obtained through the Pharmacy Research Ethics Committee (PREC) by the Islamia University of Bahawalpur, Pakistan (Reference: 166-2023-/PHEC, dated Feb 09, 2023).
Delphi process
Selection of Delphi questionnaire items.

The scientific committee conducted a systematic review of the literature, encompassing pertinent clinical guidelines, and assessments related to the management of anticoagulation and the impact of anticoagulation stewardship on patient health outcomes. After a thorough and critical examination of the pertinent literature and drawing upon their expertise in anticoagulation, the scientific committee convened in-person meetings to formulate the initial array of domains and items for the Delphi survey questionnaire.
Selection of Delphi participants.

The expert scientific committee comprised five members, including three cardiologists and two professors who were experienced and recognized in anticoagulation therapy management. In total, 90 cardiologists from various hospitals across Pakistan were approached initially and asked to participate in the study as the Delphi panel. The email IDs of target participants were obtained from publicly accessible resources, peers, published academic manuscripts, and/or institutional websites. The selection of experts was based on their substantial expertise and understanding of anticoagulation treatment. During the study, the participants were told that their participation may include numerous rounds (e.g., Round 1 and Round 2), with each round expected to last approximately 15-20 minutes. During Round 1, the participants were also requested to provide their demographic information (i.e., age, gender, type of hospital, hospital position, research experience, and work experience). The participants did not receive any compensation for their time or involvement in the study. Before sending the Delphi survey to all participants, each round was piloted with 5-6 members from the expert group to confirm that the information and queries were comprehensible. The Delphi expert panel also received participant's information pack (PIC) (i.e., participant information sheet, informed consent, and informed consent declaration - S1 File), a detailed leaflet that explained the study's objectives and procedures and an online link to the survey. Online participation in survey meant that they have read PIC and leaflet explaining the study objectives. Ethics committee (PREC) approved this consent procedure.
In the absence of agreement regarding the ideal size of a Delphi group, it is frequently observed that groups consisting of 15-50 participants are sufficient.
Round 1: Idea generation.

The members of the Delphi expert panel were asked to rate their level of agreement with each questionnaire item on a 3-point Likert scale (agree/neutral/disagree) (questionnaire developed in the first step of the Delphi process). Panelists were additionally prompted to offer remarks on each item. The scientific committee convened face-to-face meetings during which the findings of the survey were presented and deliberated. The selection of items for further deliberations was determined by the endorsement of items by 66.6% of the Delphi expert panel, in conjunction with the consensus of the scientific committee.

The items that did not gain a 66.6% level of agreement were either eliminated or revised according to the feedback received from the Delphi expert panel. Following the completion of Round 1 and the subsequent summarization of Delphi expert feedback, modifications were carried out for certain items within the questionnaire. Redundant statements were consolidated and streamlined, while issues related to the clarity of specific statements were addressed based on Delphi expert input. Additionally, new items were created and incorporated as deemed necessary. The revised survey questionnaire was then distributed again to the panelists for Round 2.
Round 2: Developing consensus.

In Round 2, the same cardiologists (Delphi expert panel) were requested to assess the set of revised/amended items from Round 1 by applying the same voting procedure as in the prior round. For this assessment, the cardiologists received a summary of the anonymously expressed views from their peers (Round 1) and any supplementary data that the scientific committee considered pertinent for facilitating consensus among the panelists. Therefore, the panelists could reflect on the group's answers following the first round and reconsider the non-consensus items based on the views of other panelists. Following the analysis of Round 2 responses, the statements that did not gain experts' consensus were kept for further discussion in Round 3.
Round 3: Confirming consensus.

This round comprised face-to-face meetings among the scientific committee to evaluate those statements that failed to gain agreement in Round 2. The participants of the scientific committee deliberated the non-consensus statements till an agreement was achieved to keep or remove these items from the final document.
Statistical analysis

SPSS 20.0 (IBM Statistics, Armonk, NY, United States) was used for data analysis. Descriptive statistical analysis such as median (range), frequencies and percentage were performed to describe characteristics of the Delphi experts.
Results
Delphi panel

Of the 90 cardiologists from 30 hospitals, 75 (83% response rate) agreed to participate in the first round of the Delphi study. Of these, 68 cardiologists participated in the Round 2 assessment. All participants were male with a median age and work experience of 48 and 12 years, respectively. Most of the participants (n = 63, 84%) were from the public sector hospitals (Table 1).

The panel members assessed 33 items from the following 4 domains: 1) Essential Components Needed to Strengthen an Anticoagulant Stewardship Program (11 items), 2) Current Status of Anticoagulant Stewardship Program in Pakistan (5 items), 3) Impact of an Anticoagulant Stewardship Program (9 items), 4) Constraints in the Implementation of the Anticoagulant Stewardship Program (8 items) (See S1 Table).
Round 1

In Round 1, a total of 18 items (54%) out of 33 items reached a consensus point without any modification. Eight out of eleven items (72.7%) from domain 1, "Essential Components Needed to Strengthen an Anticoagulant Stewardship Program"; one out of five items (20%) from domain 2, "Current Status of Anticoagulant Stewardship Program in Pakistan"; six out of nine items (66.6%) from domain 3, "Impact of an Anticoagulant Stewardship Program"; three out of eight items (60%) from domain 4, "Constraints in the Implementation of the Anticoagulant Stewardship Program" reached a consensus after getting 66.6% acceptance by the Delphi expert panel (n = 75).

A total of 15 non-consensus items were identified after Round 1. Among these, four items were thematically similar and were merged into two new items by the expert committee after considering feedback from the Delphi expert panel (cardiologist). The first merged item -merger of item 10 (Domain 1) and item 16 (Domain 2) -resulted in the statement:

"The existing practices on anticoagulants are recommended by the cardiologists, suggesting no need for an ASP program." However, this merged item failed to reach consensus even after modification and was therefore removed. The second merged item -merger of item 28 and item 30 (both from Domain 4) -resulted in the statement:

"The inconsistent guidelines and institutional policies make it difficult to implement ASP." This item was retained for reassessment in Round 2. In total, five non-consensus items that achieved a consensus of less than 40% were removed, including the first merged item (S2 Table). The remaining 8 non-consensus items, comprising seven original and one merged item, were carried forward to Round 2 (S3 Table).
Round 2

A total of 68 Delphi experts participated in Round 2. During the process, 8 (7 original and 1 merged) non-consensus items in Round 1 were again presented to the cardiologists for further discussion and agreement. Out of these, 4 items finally reached an agreement in Round 2 after a detailed discussion with the scientific committee. Four consensus items included 2 items from domain 1, "Essential components needed to strengthen an ASP" and one item each from domain 3, "Impact of an ASP" and domain 4 "Constraints in the implementation of the ASP". The remaining four non-consensus items (items 25, 32, 27, and 29) were taken to the next round for further discussion.
Round 3

Four items that failed to reach consensus in Round 2 were deliberated in Round 3 by the scientific committee, where two items were finally accepted (i.e., one item each from domain 3 "Impact of an ASP" and domain 4, "Constraints in the implementation of the ASP"). Two items were rejected from Domain 4 (items 27 and 29). After the Delphi process was finalized, 24 consensus points were ultimately selected. Fig 2 shows the results of the Delphi study.
Results of the Delphi study.

The final 24 items included 10 statements for domain 1, one statement for domain 2, eight statements for domain 3, and five statements for domain 4. Table 2 summarizes the findings from cardiologists.

Discussion

To the best of our knowledge, this is probably the first study from Pakistan that described the potential for implementation of ASP in Pakistan. Globally, the implementation of ASP improved clinical outcomes, promoted patient safety, and supported healthcare systems in delivering high-quality, evidence-based anticoagulation management. Using a Delphi technique, we developed consensus-driven recommendations for the implementation of ASP with an aim to promote rational use of anticoagulation therapy in Pakistani healthcare settings.

The present study indicated absolute agreement among Pakistani cardiologists regarding the implementation of ASP in Pakistan. A considerable consensus was achieved about the essential components needed to strengthen ASP for anticoagulation management in the cardiology departments. The expert views were generally in line with the positive impact of ASP on patients' morbidity and mortality rates associated with cardiovascular diseases. However, this study revealed that there were some constraints regarding the implementation of ASP, which must be optimized based on the standard recommendations.

More than 90% of cardiologists agreed that hospital staff should collaborate with health authorities and there must be representatives from key areas such as pharmacy, data analysis, and administrative leadership for the successful implementation of ASP. This statement is strongly endorsed in the literature. A recent study from the US further elaborated that the essential step to promote, implement, and sustain ASP was to secure partnership with administrative leadership. The existing literature also evidenced educational sessions with cardiologists, comprehensive education among patients, and training of ASP team for successful implementation of ASP in healthcare settings. This is in line with the findings of our study. The agreement of our study participants regarding the availability of a checklist for standardized core elements of ASP in hospitals further highlighted the need to foster optimal anticoagulation management, which is consistent with the published literature. Pakistan is a resource-limited country that only spends 2.9% of its GDP on healthcare. Therefore, investment in value-added programs such as ASP is minimal. However, there is a need to invest in healthcare programs, which may result in future cost savings. The same is being reported by our study participants.

There was considerable agreement among study participants on the positive impact of ASP on the patients and the healthcare system. They endorsed that this program not only focuses on patient health outcomes, such as reducing ADRs (severe bleeding events and thromboembolic events), promoting routine INR monitoring, and decreasing morbidity and mortality rates, but also decreases the workload on healthcare providers, as consistently noted in literature. Moreover, our study participants also agreed that ASP provide key training and information opportunities to healthcare providers and patients, thereby improving treatment decisions and patient adherence. This is consistent with recently published studies on the need for essential ASP educational trainings. Continuous medical education is a part of routine clinical practice in Pakistan; however, training opportunities specific to the needs of ASP are lacking.

passages.text: The Delphi panel unanimously agreed that the regulatory authorities and policymakers were not focused on the implementation of ASP, which is also reported in the recent studies. The panelists further stated that the inconsistent guidelines and institutional policies made it difficult to implement ASP. Evidence-based implementation of ASP in Pakistan is problematic due to limited industry-academia linkage. Moreover, healthcare programs and departments seldom conduct operational and implementation research (OR and IR) for process improvement. This is partly due to a lack of trained OR staff and limited funding opportunities for trainings, workshops, and conferences. The participants in this study also agreed that lack of funding led to limited training and educational activities.
Impact of findings on policy and practice

This Delphi study presents consensus points specifically from cardiologists for the implementation of ASP in Pakistan. To overcome the barriers associated with the implementation of ASP, several key components were proposed. The most effective way to address the situation was to allocate financial resources for the development of anticoagulation stewardship activities. Additionally, since the clinicians are one of the key people in the management of anticoagulants, therefore, they must have training opportunities to improve their knowledge and skills. It is also recommended that electronic guidelines for the healthcare workforce should be developed that are easily accessible and provide up-to-date protocols for anticoagulation management. Additionally, a healthcare facility-specific core elements checklist should be created to improve patient outcomes, ensuring that all parameters are consistently monitored during the treatment. This approach would streamline the decision-making and improve the quality of care.

From a practice perspective, the implementation of this program is necessary to optimize the anticoagulation therapy, minimize the escalating adverse drug reaction-related issues, reduce morbidity and mortality rates, and decrease the burden on healthcare providers. In order to achieve these objectives, a multidisciplinary team effort is required. It will be crucial to gather the perspectives of all relevant stakeholders, such as clinicians, pharmacists, patients, and policymakers, to comprehend the possible challenges of implementing this program in Pakistan. Further, studies can also focus on the implementation of ASP through the IR cycle and see how it works.
Strengths and limitations

This study has notable strengths, including a high response rate, keen involvement of cardiologists, and a high agreement rate. The comparatively cohesive opinions manifested by the cardiologists suggest that the findings include extensive relevance to the implementation of ASP. Further strengths comprise the execution of protocols aligned with standard Delphi frameworks, including confidentiality of feedback, open-ended statement creation and progressive development of items, and stability assessments of items in various rounds.

There are a few limitations to the study. First, the findings of the study may not be generalized for other countries based on the fact every country has her own healthcare system and needs. Second, only cardiologists were part of this study, while the viewpoints of policymakers and other healthcare professionals such as pharmacists, nurses, etc., were not obtained. We did not include other healthcare professionals because their inclusion was not meaningful due to their limited role in clinical and administrative matters of healthcare delivery. Third, this study did not evaluate the feasibility and affordability of implementing ASP under this project.
Conclusion

This Delphi study developed 24 consensus points for implementing ASP in Pakistan. The Delphi members suggested the essential components needed to strengthen ASP. This study acknowledged strategies to implement ASP, including educational sessions for patients and healthcare professionals, collaboration with healthcare authorities, and allocation of financial resources. This study also identified consensus of cardiologists on the perceived benefits of ASP for patients and the healthcare system. Several barriers that have hindered the implementation of ASP in Pakistan were identified, including patient- and healthcare system-related barriers.

passages.text: Research note: Comparison of apparent and standardized ileal digestibility of amino acids in corn-soybean meal-based diets for laying hens at different ages

This study aimed to assess and compare the apparent ileal digestibility (AID) and standardized ileal digestibility (SID) of amino acids (AA) in laying hens at different ages. A total of 180 28-wk-old Hy-Line Brown laying hens were randomly assigned to 3 age groups of 30, 50, and 70 wks. At each designated age, 60 hens were randomly allotted to 2 treatment diets: nitrogen-free diet (NFD) for estimating basal endogenous losses (BEL) of AA and corn-soybean meal-based diet (CSD). It was observed that the BEL of most AA increased with age, with significant increases (P < 0.05) for Arg, Lys, Thr, Asp, and Ser by an average of 118.3 % for these 5 AA in 70-wk-old hens than in 30-wk-old hens. The AID and SID of most AA in CSD decreased as hens were aged, with 70-wk-old hens exhibiting significant reductions (P < 0.05) in the AID of Arg and Lys by an average of 10.4 %, and in the SID of these 2 AA by 7.6 % compared with 30-wk-old hens. The AID and SID of Met were also lower (P < 0.05) in 70-wk-old hens by an average of 12.5 % and 10.7 %, respectively, than in both 30-wk-old and 50-wk-old hens. In conclusion, the BEL of AA increased, whereas AA digestibility decreased with advancing age in laying hens. Specifically, 70-wk-old hens showed decreased digestibility of limiting AA (Arg, Lys, and Met) compared with younger hens. Therefore, age-dependent AA digestibility in laying hens should be considered to improve the precision of feed formulation.
Introduction

Accurate estimation of amino acid (AA) availability in poultry diets is essential to improve the precision of feed formulation, ensuring that AA requirements are satisfied while minimizing nitrogen excretion. The AA availability in poultry diets is commonly assessed using apparent ileal digestibility (AID) or standardized ileal digestibility (SID; ). It is well-documented that AA digestibility in poultry is influenced by various factors, including methodology used for digestibility determination, feed compositions, and animal characteristics such as sex, genotype, and health status. One potential animal factor affecting AA digestibility is the age because the ability of poultry to digest and absorb dietary AA varies with age. It has been recognized that AA digestibility generally increases with advancing age in broiler chickens, likely due to progressive improvements in digestive physiology. However, despite the potential effect of age on AA digestibility in laying hens, relevant information is largely limited. A previous study using cecectomized hens reported that increasing age of hens improved apparent total tract digestibility of AA. In contrast, observed decreased apparent total tract retention of DM and CP, along with increased AA excretion as laying hens were aged. This contradictory finding may result from variations in methodology, feed compositions, and animals between these studies. However, these studies examined the effect of age on apparent AA digestibility without accounting for endogenous AA losses, potentially complicating AA digestibility in laying hens at different ages. The SID of AA is considered a more accurate estimate of AA digestibility than AID of AA in poultry. However, to our knowledge, no studies have investigated the effect of age on the SID of AA in laying hens. Therefore, this study aimed to assess and compare the AID and SID of AA in laying hens across 3 different ages.

passages.text: NFD, nitrogen-free diet; CSD, corn-soybean meal-based diet.

Provided per kg of the complete diet: vitamin A, 12,000 IU; vitamin D3, 4,000 IU; vitamin E, 80.0 mg; vitamin K3, 4.0 mg; vitamin B1, 4.0 mg; vitamin B2, 10.0 mg; vitamin B6, 6.0 mg; vitamin B12, 20.0 microg; folic acid, 2.0 mg; biotin, 200 microg; niacin, 60 mg.

Provided per kg of the complete diet: iron, 60 mg (FeSO4); zinc, 100 mg (ZnSO4); manganese, 120 mg (MnO); copper, 16 mg (CuSO4); cobalt, 1,000 microg (CoSO4); selenium, 300 microg (Na2SeO3); iodine, 1.25 mg [Ca(IO3)2].

All experimental procedures were reviewed and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Chung-Ang University (Approval No. 202401030073). A total of 180 28-wk-old Hy-Line Brown laying hens (average BW = 1.93 +- 0.07 kg) originated from the same flock were randomly assigned to 3 age groups at 30, 50, and 70 wks of age. All hens were individually housed in a cage (24 x 36 x 39 cm) in an environmentally-controlled room and fed a commercial layer diet until the designated age for determination of AA digestibility. At each age, 60 hens of each age group were randomly allotted to 2 treatment diets: nitrogen-free diet (NFD) and corn-soybean meal-based diet (CSD). The NFD treatment had 3 replicates with 8 hens per replicate, whereas the CSD treatment had 6 replicates with 6 hens per replicate. The NFD was prepared to estimate the basal endogenous losses (BEL) of AA (; Table 1). The CSD was formulated as a typical layer diet primarily with corn and soybean meal (SBM) according to the nutrient requirement estimates for laying hens. The identical formulation for CSD was maintained across all age groups to eliminate possible factors other than age. However, the prolonged duration of this study (i.e., 40 wks) precluded the use of a single batch of corn and SBM for all age groups. Accordingly, to minimize nutritional variability, corn and SBM from the same country of origin (i.e., imported corn from USA and domestic SBM from South Korea) with comparable particle size and nutritional compositions were used in all age groups. The analyzed concentrations of CP and AA in corn, SBM, NFD, and CSD for each age are presented in Table 1. Chromium oxide was used as an indigestible marker at 0.50 % in all diets. Environmental conditions, including ambient temperature and photoperiod, were controlled according to the management guideline of.
Ileal digesta collection and chemical analysis

At each age, hens in CSD treatments were fed CSD for 10 d, whereas those in NFD treatment were fed NFD for 5 d before ileal digesta collection. Hens were given free access to diets and water. Sample collection and digesta processing were performed as described previously.

The treatment diets and ileal digesta were analyzed for DM (method 930.15) and CP (method 984.13). The concentrations of AA in diets and digesta were quantified using an l-8900 AA analyzer (Hitachi, Tokyo, Japan; method 982.30). Briefly, samples were hydrolyzed with 6 N HCl at 110  C for 24 h, concentrated, buffered, and filtered before ion-exchange chromatography with post-column ninhydrin detection. Sulfur-containing AA were measured after performic-acid oxidation, whereas Trp was analyzed from separate alkaline hydrolysates. The concentrations of Cr were measured after wet-acid digestion by inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES; Optima 5300 DV, PerkinElmer, Shelton, CT; method 985.01). All analyses were conducted in triplicate.
Calculations and statistical analysis
The values for BEL, AID, and SID of AA were determined on a DM basis, following calculations of ileal AA digestibility based on the index method.

All data were analyzed by ANOVA using the MIXED procedure of SAS (SAS Institute, Cary, NC). Each replicate was considered the experimental unit. The LSMEANS procedure was used to calculate treatment means and Tukey's honestly significant difference test was used to separate treatment means. Significance for statistical tests was set at P < 0.05.
Results and discussion
Basal endogenous losses (BEL) of amino acids (AA) and digestibility of AA in corn-soybean meal-based diets for laying hens at 30, 50, and 70 wks of age1.

passages.text: a,bMeans with different superscripts in a row differ significantly (P < 0.05).
Basal endogenous losses are the means of 3 replications, whereas digestibility values are the means of 6 replications.
AID, apparent ileal digestibility; SID, standardized ileal digestibility.

The BEL of most AA in laying hens generally increased with age from 30 to 70 wks, although significance was observed only for Arg, Lys, Thr, Asp, and Ser (Table 2). The BEL of Arg, Thr, and Ser was greater (P < 0.05) in 70-wk-old hens than in 30-wk-old hens by 74.1 %, 72.1 %, and 113.2 %, respectively, with 50-wk-old hens showing intermedicate values. However, the BEL of Lys and Asp in hens at both 50 and 70 wks of age was greater (P < 0.05) than in hens at 30 wk of age. Compared with 30-wk-old hens, 50-wk-old hens exhibited increases in the BEL of Lys and Asp by 149.1 % and 110.3 %, respectively, whereas 70-wk-old hens showed even greater increases of 177.5 % and 154.5 %.

The predominant AA in the BEL of laying hens were Glu, Asp, Leu, Thr, and Ser, despite the slight age-related variation in this study, which is consistent with the previous findings. The observation of increased BEL of most AA with age may result from age-related alterations in intestinal structure and function of laying hens. Aged hens have been reported to show decreased efficiency of nutrient digestion and absorption, leading to a compensatory increase in intestinal morphology and enzyme secretion. These compensatory changes may enhance intestinal cell losses and digestive enzyme excretion, thereby elevating the BEL of AA. In particular, age-dependent increases in the BEL of Arg, Lys, Thr, Asp, and Ser were significant. This effect on Thr, Asp, and Ser may be caused by their high abundance in mucins and related secretions, with advancing age leading to enhanced mucosal turnover. However, the reason for significant increases in the BEL of Arg and Lys is not clear; however, it may be related to decreased expression of intestinal cationic AA transporters with aging, which may reduce reabsorption of endogenous Arg and Lys losses.

The AID and SID of most AA in CSD decreased with age, with 4 AAs (Arg, Lys, Met, and Trp) being significantly affected. In 70-wk-old hens compared with 30-wk-old hens, the AID of Arg and Lys decreased (P < 0.05) by 8.1 % and 12.6 %, respectively, while the SID of Arg and Lys also declined (P < 0.05) by 6.4 % and 8.9 %. However, the AID and SID of Arg and Lys in 50-wk-old hens did not differ from other age groups. The AID and SID of Met were lower (P < 0.05) in 70-wk-old hens than in hens at both 30 and 50 wks of age, with average reductions of 12.5 % and 10.7 %, respectively. The AID of Trp in CSD in 70-wk-old hens was lower (P < 0.05) by 5.1 % than in 30-wk-old hens despite no differences compared with 50-wk-old hens; however, the SID of Trp did not differ among hens at different ages.

A previous study reported increased AA digestibility with advancing age in cecectomized hens from 27 to 57 wks, possibly due to increasing development of intestinal structure and function. In contrast, reported that increasing age of hens from 27 to 75 wks decreased apparent DM and CP retention with elevated AA losses in excreta as a consequence of decreased efficiency of nutrient digestion and absorption. This result is consistent with the current findings of decreased AID of N and most AA with age. In this study, the BEL of most AA increased with age, which may partly explain decreased AID of AA with age because an increase in the BEL of AA typically contributes to decreased AID of AA. However, after correcting AID for the BEL of AA measured at each age, the SID of most AA also decreased with age, indicating that AA digestion and absorption actually decreased with advancing age of hens. This observation is likely attributable to the reduction in digestive enzyme secretion and its activity with increasing age of hens. Moreover, decreased expressions of intestinal AA transporters with age may also be possible reason for these findings. Nevertheless, the information regarding age-dependent changes in AA absorptive capacity is lacking, especially in laying hens, which limits further interpretation. In this study, 70-wk-old hens showed a significant decline in the SID of Arg, Lys, and Met, typically considered limiting AAs for chickens, compared with 30-wk-old hens. The reason for significant reductions in only these 3 AAs remains unclear; however, it may indicate that application of a single SID value for these AAs in layer diet formulations, regardless of age, may lead to an under- or over-estimation of most essential AA concentrations in diets because essential AAs are formulated based on ideal protein concepts.

In conclusion, the BEL of most AA in laying hens increased with age, whereas the AID and SID of most AA in CSD decreased. In particular, compared with 30-wk-old hens, 70-wk-old hens exhibited a greater BEL of AA, averaging a 57.8 % increase, while decreased AID and SID of AA in CSD by an average of 6.0 % and 4.0 %, respectively, suggesting that applications of age-dependent AA digestibility in laying hens are necessary to improve the precision of feed formulations.

passages.text: An in silico approach for screening non-synonymous SNPs in Mycobacterium tuberculosis PPE68 protein and impact on structure

PPE68 has been implicated through computational methods in ethambutol (EMB) resistance, plausibly through gene-gene interactions with embA. The interest of the current study was to use in silico approaches to gain insights into the effects of mutations on the structure and function of PPE68. Drug-resistant clinical isolate sequences from the NCBI Database were studied. PPE68 missense nsSNPs were analysed using bioinformatics tools. Isolated sequences which harboured mutations that could be key in driving a drug-resistant phenotype were selected for structural modelling and molecular dynamics simulations- mutations likely occurring in conserved regions of the N-terminal domain, including A26T/Q92K, L163F/L167R, L167P, L167R and E44G. The 83 sequences that were aligned exhibited some clustering with an interest on the variants A26T/Q92K, L167P, L167R and L163F/L167R appearing to cluster together, with the exception of E44G. There was a significant shift in the conformation of the mutants with A26T/Q92K (9.99 +- 2.05 A) and L167P (10.03 +- 2.14 A), undergoing the greatest change. L163F/L167R and A26T/Q92K displayed the most stability, whilst being the most loosely packed. This is in contrast to the unstable E44G, L167P and L167R which were more compact than the wildtype. Considering that the PPE family of proteins are highly disordered in their native form and presumably in their most stable conformation, these outcomes are conceivable.
Introduction

Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tb) is an etiological agent of tuberculosis (TB) that has caused 1.3 million deaths in 2022, whilst an alarming 3.1 million infections were either undiagnosed or not reported. M. tb thrives by continuously evolving intricate mechanisms to evade the host's defence system, as well as acquiring resistance to therapeutic and prophylactic interventions. Drug resistance is a major health threat that undermines global efforts to combat TB. Development of mutations to known targets of both first- and second-line anti-TB drugs has been evident, requiring digression toward the use of more innovative diagnostic, therapeutic and prophylactic tools. The prevalence of ethambutol (EMB) resistance ranges between 7.1 and 58% in patients presenting with multidrug resistant TB (MDR-TB). Moreover, this display of heterogeneity in pathology, microbiology and immunological response makes it difficult to identify suitable biomarkers for both diagnosis and treatment of M. tb.

Amongst the sophisticated and specialized functional systems of M. tb, the type VII secretion system (T7SSs), which harnesses the PE-PPE/PGRS family of proteins in the ESX-1 subtype, is essential for virulence. The conserved Pro-Glu (PE) and Pro-Pro-Glu (PPE) motif is a distinctive signature of the N-terminal domain of the Mycobacterium protein. This family of proteins is defined by largely disordered structural motifs, which undergo a significant shift to more ordered and folded structures upon complex formation, as described for the PPE68-PE35 and PPE65-PE32 dimerization. Moreover, the co-transcription and co-translation of PPE65-PE32 has been shown to inhibit the immune response against M. tb by altering the THP-1 response. The PE-PPE family of proteins codes for approximately 10% of the Mycobacteria genome, and despite the decline in the genome size of M. tb, the gain in pathogenesis has been paralleled by the expansion of the PE-PPE genes. The PE-PPE proteins have been implicated in 60% of gene pairs associated with drug resistance, whereby one TB drug target and a member of the PPE family were identified coincidingly through computational methods. PPE68 was reported to pair with embA - an ethambutol (EMB) drug target associated with resistance.

Responses to selective pressures and homologous recombination between the N-terminal domains of the PE and PPE attribute to the observed high mutation rates within this family of proteins. The evolutionary trajectory of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the PPE68 genome, including their role in drug resistance, has not been exhaustively investigated and established, as well as the implications of their convergent or divergent characteristics in acquiring drug resistance. Interestingly, the PE-PPE family harbours most of the homoplastic SNPs identified in the genome of M. tb compared to other families, reportedly 36%, however, more than 50% display non-homoplasticity - suggesting diversity in the evolutionary functions of the proteins. Homoplastic non-synonymous SNPs (nsSNPs) are mainly associated with PPE18, PPE19, PPE57, PPE59 and PPE60, suggesting a negating evolutionary pattern for PPE68. Therefore, there is a gap in knowledge that provides an in-depth understanding of the role of PPE68 nsSNPs in the mechanisms acquired by M. tb to resist drug therapy.

The potential role of PPE68 in the mechanism of M. tb EMB drug resistance has not yet been explored, which is the interest of the current study. It is important to channel more research into gaining insights into the role of PPE68 in M. tb's strategy in acquiring EMB resistance. Whether these proteins function as accessories to the already known and characterised drug targets, or drive resistance through distinctive functional roles is important to distinguish for designing and delivering innovative approaches for managing TB infections.
Results
Characterization of the nsSNPs and phylogenetic analysis

Prominent and missense nsSNPs identified from the drug-resistant isolates and their prevalence are represented in Tables 1 and 2. nsSNPs that occurred in the conserved N-terminal were prominent in the A29, V73 and Q92 locations. Within the group of missense nsSNPs, L167 occurrences accounted for 5% which was in the majority (Table 2).

A phylogenetic tree was constructed to assess whether the 83 aligned sequences exhibited homoplasy as a consequence of exposure to similar selection pressures, potentially arising from anti-TB drugs. The results from the phylogenetic tree (Fig. 1) showed that the sequences harbouring the nsSNPs originated from common ancestry. Some convergent patterns were also observed, including the variants that were selected for downstream analysis, which are highlighted in Fig. 1. Additionally, some of the sequences did cluster with the M. tb RGTB423 strain (Accession number: AFE14949.1). This strain was isolated from a sputum sample of a TB patient as part of a drug screening programme in Kerala, India.

Identification of mutations with potential effects on the structure-function

nsSNPs that were selected for further analysis were identified by carrying out MSA of the 83 TB drug-resistant clinical isolate sequences, wherein hydrophobic residues that were mutated in the highly conserved N-terminal domain were identified. Hydrophobic interactions are amongst the most crucial for stabilizing proteins, therefore, isolate sequences harbouring hydrophobic nsSNPs in the conserved N-terminal region were selected foremost. Subsequently, 34 sequences were chosen, and to refine this selection further, the GRAVY score (Grand Average of Hydropathy) for each sequence was computed. The GRAVY scores were all above zero, showing variations (Fig. 2).

Furthermore, a comparative analysis was done, whereby the intrinsic physicochemical properties of the original amino acid versus the substituent residue were considered in selecting the 10 sequences that showed the possibility of posing the most detrimental effects on the structure and stability, potentially affecting the function of PPE68. Figure 3 shows the alignment of these sequences to the parent sequence, AFN51902.1. Finally, five nsSNPs were chosen from predicting and ranking their potential impact on the stability of PPE68 for continuation with MD analysis. The DUET and NeEMO computational programs were used for predicting the change in stability caused by the mutations (Table 3).

For the final selection of variants, preference was given to mutants that had the most impact on the GRAVY score and stability. According to the GRAVY score, the hydropathy index for E44G (CKP03726.1) showed the greatest hydrophobicity, and this mutant also showed increased stability (Table 3). Interestingly, only E44G did not exhibit phylogenetic clustering with the other four variants chosen for MD analysis. Therefore, E44G was selected for comparative analysis with the other mutants, which resulted in decreased hydrophobicity of PPE68. A decrease in hydrophobicity was also observed with L163F/L167R (WP_057347446.1), L167R (WP_057132601.1), L167P (WP_057332050.1) and A26T/Q92K (WP_057361361.1), respectively. Moreover, these mutants were preferable since they were representative of the nsSNPs that were prominent (Tables 1 and 2), and they were also predicted to induce instability (Table 3).

Structural modelling of PPE68 and mutants

In the absence of protein crystal structures, homology modelling is an inexpensive and easy method used to computationally determine the three-dimensional (3D) structure of proteins. The AlphaFold server was used to determine the 3D structure of the PPE68 protein and the selected mutants (Fig. 4). PPE68 and mutants are approximately 368 amino acids long and predominantly adopt alpha-helical structures (Fig. 4). This is in agreement with the secondary structure analysis using PSIPred, depicting mostly alpha-helical conformations. The disordered regions which are intrinsic to PPE68 were identified through PSIPred wildtype and mutant proteins, and these regions are highlighted by the grey regions in the plot (Fig. 4).

The structure of PPE68 and mutants modelled using the AlphaFold server. The N-terminal domain in each model is coloured purple and the mutations are highlighted in red. The Ramachandran plots were obtained from the VADAR v1.8 server and represent the core (red), allowed (yellow), generous (green) and disallowed regions (grey). Secondary structure analysis using the PSIPred server highlighted the alpha-helices in pink and beta-sheets in yellow

Table 4 shows the scores that were used to assess the modelled structures. The Rama Z-score compares a set of high-resolution structures to the model, and scores between - 2 and 2 indicate a normal protein backbone. The ERRAT overall quality factor for the models is greater than 50, indicating that these structures are of good quality (Table 4). The MolProbity score combines the clash score, rotamer and Ramachandran evaluations, and lower MolProbity scores are indicative of better-quality structures. The modelled structures are of good quality, as it is expected that a good model would have over 90% of residues in the most favoured regions.

passages.text: Evaluating local interactions formed by the residues in the wildtype versus the mutant PPE68

In this study, the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database was used to analyse the plausible alterations on the local interactions formed with the neighbouring residues subsequent to mutations. The mutants that were assessed included E44G, A26T/Q92K, L167P, L167R and L163F/L167R (Fig. 5).

The E44 residue in the wildtype PPE68 makes three hydrogen bonds (H-bonds) with Q41 and R48. This differs in the E44G mutant, wherein G44 makes an additional hydrogen bond with A42 (Fig. 5). The non-conservative substitutions A26T/Q92K led to hydrogen bonding patterns different to the wildtype, wherein A26 makes hydrogen bonds with A22, A29 and G30, whilst the polar T26 acquired new H-bonds with P23 and A27, but with G30 remaining the same. In the Q92 position, glutamine makes H-bonds with the proximal residues Q88, A94, A95 and with Q92/itself (Fig. 5). In contrast, the positively charged lysine residue with a longer hydrocarbon chain displayed H-bonds with the amino acids T90, A91, A93 and again with A94.

L167 forms no hydrogen bonds with any of the nearby residues, and this was also true when a proline substitution (L167P) was made, which likewise is a non-polar uncharged amino acid. However, the positively charged arginine in the same position (L167R) resulted in formation of two hydrogen bonds with E165 located in the same polypeptide chain (Fig. 5). Interestingly, introducing L163F in the same variant, that is, L163F/L167R breaks both of the hydrogen bonds between R167 and E165. Moreover, in the native protein L163 makes hydrogen bonds with the same E165, whereas in the double mutant L163F/L167R, F163 makes hydrogen bonds with T162. This suggests that the L163F may be a compensatory mutation.
Local interactions and hydrogen bonding patterns of the selected residues in the variants versus wildtype PPE86
N-terminal domain molecular dynamics simulations of the wildtype PPE68 and variants

To investigate the effect of the mutations on the N-terminal domain of PPE68, the dynamic behaviour and stability of the modelled structures was investigated by performing molecular dynamic (MD) simulations and post-dynamic analyses. The compactness of protein structures which is represented by the Rg, refers to how secondary structures are packed into the tertiary structure. The Rg of the PPE68 structure and the mutant structures all stay within 1 A, this indicates that the structures are relatively compact and stable (Fig. 6A). However, the native structure becomes more compact in the presence of the L167P mutation (WP_057332050.1) from Rg value of 43.59 +- 0.17 A to 40.99 +- 0.22 A. In contrast, the L163F/L167R (WP_057347446.1) and the A26T/Q92K mutations (WP_057361361.1) assume relatively less compact structures with Rg values of 44.44 +- 0.18 A and 44.53 +- 0.20 A, respectively. Figure 6B shows the potential energy profiles to compare the trajectory of the protein alpha carbons (Calpha). The shift in potential energy values for the L163F/L167R and A26T/Q92K mutations suggest stabilising effects. The RMSD and the RMSF values were calculated to investigate the dynamic nature of the proteins. Figure 6C shows the RMSD values of the proteins which increases for the mutated proteins compared to PPE68 protein (5.98 +- 1.10 A). This increase indicates that the mutations undergo significant conformational changes in comparison to the wildtype with the A26T/Q92K (9.99 +- 2.05 A) and L167P (10.03 +- 2.14 A) mutations undergoing the greatest conformational changes. Figure 6D shows the protein RMSF values which are used to identify the contribution of amino acids to protein flexibility. The flexibility of the individual amino acids does not vary greatly amongst the wildtype and mutations. The highest flexibility however is observed for the L163F/L167R mutant between residues 100 and 150.

Molecular dynamics simulations of N-terminal domain of PPE68 and its mutants. The (A) radius of gyration, (B) potential energy, (C) RMSD, and (D) RMSF of the simulations were analysed following molecular dynamic analysis. The wildtype PPE68 was included as a reference. The variants included CKP03726.1 (E44G), WP_057132601.1 (L167R), WP_057332050.1 (L167P), WP_057347446.1 (L163F/L167R) and WP_057361361.1 (A26T/Q92K)

The electrostatic potential and fraction accessible surface area (FASA) were evaluated (Fig. 7). Notably, the mutations in PPE68 induced notable changes in surface charge distribution and solvent exposure. PPE68 displayed a balanced electrostatic landscape, while the mutants showed localised shifts in charge intensity and polarity. The subtle variations observed in the FASA profiles suggests that PPE68 mutations changed the degree of residue solvent accessibility reflecting local conformational adjustments. These findings correspond with the observed MD data and suggest that the mutations modulate the PPE68's surface properties and influence stability and dynamics.

Assessing the potential deleterious effect of nsSNPs

The potential deleterious effects of the nsSNPs were predicted using various tools and then summarised in Table 5. With the SNP&GO the probability scores are computed, and the variant will either be classified as neutral or diseased whereas with the SIFT a score between 0 and 0.05 represents intolerability, whilst a score closer to 1 indicates tolerability. These scores are accompanied by computation of a positive predictive/confidence analysis value. Lastly, the PolyPhen2 analysis tool which gives an indication of the benign or damaging nature of the nsSNPs is dependent on the effect of the amino acid substitution on the structure and function of the protein. Therefore, with these tools the objective was to capture the significance of the effect of the nsSNPs induced at protein level and the potential manifestation of these alterations at the phenotypic level.

According to all three computational tools, the E44G mutation was predicted to be neutral, tolerable and benign. The SIFT analysis tool which is a measure of tolerability of the respective substitutions suggested that only the A26T and Q92K had the potential to have deleterious effects. The A26T and Q92K mutations were as well predicted to be damaging by Poly-Phen v2 as single mutants or as the double mutant A26T/Q92K. In contrast, the SNP&GO program which infers its predictions from the protein sequence, functional annotations and evolutionary information using gene ontology (GO) terms, assigned neutral effects to both A26T and Q92K. The only variants associated with pathogenicity according to the SNP&GO analysis were the L167P and L167R, whilst the latter was also validated by Poly-Phen v2. The L163F was also predicted to be pathogenic by Poly-Phen v2.
