Discussion

Much like Esat6 and CFP10, PPE68 is a highly immunogenic protein that is encoded by the Rv3873 gene which is expressed within the RD1 region of the M. tb genome however absent in the attenuated BCG vaccine. PPE68 localises predominately on the cell wall of M. tb positioning it as an easily accessible target for development of drugs, vaccines and diagnostics.

Although there was no obvious clustering pattern from the 83 sequences included in the initial analyses, the variants that were selected for further MD and structural modelling appeared to cluster together on the phylogenetic tree, except for E44G (Fig. 1). This suggests that there may be some occurring convergence toward developing similar protein functions- possibly with a goal of acquiring a drug-resistant phenotype. Moreover, homoplastic mutations have been implicated in various processes including antimicrobial resistance, virulence and immune invasion amongst others further highlighting their relevance in this study. Additionally, our selected variants emanate from the N-terminal domain of PPE68, and it has been reported that the highly conserved N-terminal domains of PE and PPE genes can engage in homologous recombination via protein-protein interactions, which is another possible reason for the appearance of the mutations.

A deeper understanding of the effect of the mutations was assessed through MD analysis and structural modelling, with the aim of gaining insight into the role of PPE68 in the mechanism of EMB resistance. Amongst the selected nsSNPs, with respect to the RMSD interpretation, the most significant conformational changes imposed on the PPE68 N-terminal region were observed with the L167P and A26T/Q92K, respectively. For the L167P this may explain the destabilizing effects of the mutant, indicating that the newly acquired interactions/bonds are unfavourable. With reference to Fig. 5, in the P167 mutant state, proximal residues now included residues S172, E168, F164 and L163. This may account for the significant shift in localised contacts with possible steric hinderances that would extend throughout the N-terminal region thereby significantly altering the structural conformation of PPE68. There were no changes in the local hydrogen bonding patterns in the mutant, which suggests that hydrogen bonds did not play a significant role in the destabilization of the L167P protein.

In contrast, the A26T/Q92K led to altered hydrogen bonding patterns, with both mutations fostering hydrogen bond contacts with amino acid residues different from the native PPE68. Consequently, the A26T/Q92K double mutant behaved indifferently to L167P, displaying increased stability with a more loosely packed structure. This also suggests that the shift in the A26T/Q92K hydrogen bonding pattern may be a compensatory mechanism. Interestingly, a different compensatory mechanism was also observed for the L163F/L167R, wherein the L163F may be a compensatory mutation - seemingly its introduction to the L167R mutant (to form the L163F/L167R) breaks the two hydrogen bonds that are acquired when replacing L167 with an arginine residue (in the wildtype PPE68 the L167 residue forms no H-bond networks). Similar to the A26T/Q92K double mutant, the L163F/L167R variant was the most stabilizing and less compact compared to the wildtype PPE68, and additionally it displayed the greatest flexibility between residues 100 and 150. In addition to hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions may also play a role in the stability of PPE68. The E44G mutant had the highest GRAVY score, larger than the wildtype PPE68 which may have contributed to its more compact structure however with destabilizing effects.

The pathophysiology of various hereditary and infectious diseases has been linked to nsSNPs that are capable of inducing significant alterations in the function of proteins, consequently creating molecular phenotypes that are characteristic of diseased states. These changes in function may be concomitant with the conformational alterations in the protein and/or defects in epigenetic modifications that are important for driving various regulatory processes and systems in the cell. The pathogenicity of the variants was predicted using multiple tools - SNP&GO, SIFT and Poly-Phen v2. In terms of protein function, the non-conservative mutations A26T and Q92K were predicted to be intolerable by SIFT, in agreement with Poly-Phen V2. Only the L167P and L167R variants were predicted to be associated with pathogenicity by SNP&GO, suggesting that L167 has an evolutionary important function in the PPE68 protein which may be associated with pathogenicity. The possible pathogenicity inducing effect by the non-conservative L167R substitution was validated by Poly-Phen v2 which takes into account the secondary and tertiary characteristics such as potential loses in hydrogen bonds (H-bonds), solvent accessibility and importance of the residue in ligand binding, and subunit interactions. Hence, based on these predictive parameters only E44G and L167P were assigned as benign by Poly-Phen v2 since both did not show significant alterations in their hydrogen bonding pattern.
Conclusions

Some variants such as the double mutants L163F/L167R and A26T/Q92K may be geared toward increasing the dimerization/multimerization probability of the PPE68 protein by increasing disordered regions. In both cases the Rg values were increased suggesting loose packing of the structures, but these mutants were the most stabilizing especially the L163F/L167R mutant, and this is despite that the L163F/L167R displayed high flexibility between residues 100 to 150. The PPE proteins are known for being structurally disordered and developing a more ordered state with increased helical content upon multimerization. The PE35-PPE68 complexation has been characterized, and in the study, the N-terminal domain of PPE68 was reported to be part of the dimerization interface, with the implication of Asp/Glu/Asn/Gln as binding residues. Despite the observed increase in folding, a significant 40% remained disordered which was postulated to be the more variable C-terminal region. This also suggested that another binding event possibly exists to create a multimeric protein and/or an insertion into the membrane may occur forming channels for transport of molecules across the Mycobacterium cell wall. All this structural evidence has led to the postulation that the PE-PPE proteins may act as transport or gating systems in Mycobacterium, which may have important implications in the mechanism of PPE68 in drug resistance. Inferring from this, it is thus unsurprising that the stabilizing mutants such as A26T/Q92K and L163F/L167R assume loosely packed structures, whilst the most destabilizing E44G, L167P and L167R are more compact than the wildtype PPE68. Therefore, the A26T/Q92K and L163F/L167R variants may be driving drug resistance by promoting multimerization, forming a gating system that prevents accumulation of EMB inside the cell. Another plausible mechanism is through impacting the gene regulation pathway of embA, with the multimer binding directly to the regulatory sites or inducing signalling pathways that cause significant shifts in the levels of embA in the cell leading to a decrease in the inhibitory effect of EMB. Future work is warranted and will entail drug binding studies to assess whether PPE68 acts as off-target of EMB as another strategy for driving drug resistance.
Methodology
Data mining and identification of nsSNPs

Protein sequences of PPE68 from M. tb and the M. tb complex were retrieved from the NCBI Protein Database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/protein/). A total of 187 sequences were retrieved, downloaded in FASTA format, and stored locally for further analysis. The reference sequence used in this study was H37Rv (Rv3873; Accession: NP_218395.1), which was also obtained from NCBI. Pairwise sequence alignment was performed using BLASTp with default parameters (https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi) to compare each PPE68 sequence against the M. tb H37Rv reference sequence. Alignment results were downloaded, and sequences with large gaps or poor-quality data were excluded from further analysis. Cleaned PPE68 sequences (a total of 83) were aligned using Clustal Omega (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/Tools/msa/clustalo/) using default parameters. The alignment output was downloaded and visualized using Jalview and MEGA software.
Mutation identification and analysis

The cleaned sequences were then aligned using the Ugene software. The alignment was analysed to identify hydrophobic residues that were changed. Analysis of the N-terminal sequences (residues 1 to 175) with changed hydrophobic residues was performed using the ProtParam Tool. Aligned sequences were examined to identify stable mutations across multiple M. tb strains. Stable mutations were defined as amino acid substitutions present in multiple strains, and are located in functionally significant domains, or have potential associations with drug resistance or immune evasion. Identified conserved mutations were recorded and analysed In Silico for potential functional implications.

Mutations which could pose more disruption in the structure were further analysed using the NEtwork Enthalpic Modelling (NeEMO), DUET, and DynaMut2 server. The NeEMO server predicts the impact of point mutations on protein stability by analysing Residue Interaction Networks (RINs) by leveraging the topological features of residue interactions. The DUET server works through integration of the mutation Cutoff Scanning Matrix (mCSM) and Site-Directed Mutator (SDM) energy-based prediction methods to predict the effects of mutations. Finally, the DynaMut2 server integrates molecular dynamics-based modelling and graph-based signatures to predict the impact of single and multiple point mutations on protein stability and flexibility.
Protein modelling and analysis

To date, there is no crystal structure of PPE68, this poses a challenge in visualizing the potential effects of the mutations. In this study, the wildtype (NCBI accession: AFN51902.1) and the five variants with NCBI accession numbers WP_057347446.1 (L163F/L167R), CKP03726.1 (E44G), WP_057132601.1 (L167R), WP_057332050.1 (L167P) and WP_057361361.1 (A26T/Q92K) were modelled. The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database was used to predict the 3D structures of the protein. The modelled proteins were evaluated using the MolProbity, VADAR (Volume, Area, Dihedral Angle Reporter) version 1.8, ERRAT module on the Saves v1.6 and the SWISS MODEL structure assessment tool. The secondary structure of the sequences was analysed using the PSIPred server. The electrostatic potential and fractional accessible surface area of the wildtype PPE68 and mutants were evaluated using the APBS plugin on the Pymol server and the VADAR server, respectively.
Molecular dynamic simulations and post dynamic analysis

Molecular dynamic simulations predict the movement of atoms in a molecular system over time and can be used to predict how biomolecules respond to mutations at an atomic level. The GPU-enabled Desmond molecular dynamics simulation engine implemented on Maestro v12.2 was used to perform MD simulations on the N-terminal domain of the parent protein, and five proteins with mutations. The N-terminal domain is highly conserved, therefore mutations in this region would potentially have a greater impact on the structure and function of PPE68 with possible effects on the anti-mycobacterium immune response or drug binding if EMB does directly bind to PPE68, which we have not shown. It is also noteworthy that the N-terminal domains of PPE18, PPE57 and PPE60 interact with TRL2 of the hosts' macrophage. Furthermore, eight of the homoplastic nsSNPs were found in this region in the PPE18. Thus, it is possible that the identified nsSNPs in the PPE68 protein may confer various functions such as antigenic variability, immune evasion and drug resistance. The protein molecules were dissolved in orthorhombic water boxes with T1P3P water molecules, and periodic box dimensions were set to 10 A. The NPT ensemble (300 K and 1 bar pressure) and an OPLS forcefield was used for 100 ns. Trajectories derived from the MD simulation were then used to perform post dynamic analysis to determine the root mean square deviation (RMSD), root mean square fluctuation (RMSF), radius of gyration (Rg) and potential energy.
Predicting the deleterious effects of the mutations

Although nsSNPs may alter the protein structure and stability, these may not result in phenotypic alterations that manifest in diseased states. To predict the pathophysiological outcomes of the selected mutations, three 'pathogenicity' predictive programs, which employ different algorithms and training feature sets, were used. Selected nsSNPs were characterised using SNP&GO, SIFT (Sorting Intolerant From Tolerant) and Poly-Phen v2 (Polymorphism Phenotyping version 2).

The SNP&GO server bases its predictions on the protein sequence, evolutionary information and functional annotation through gene ontology (GO) terms. The protein sequence to be analysed is deposited into the provided User Interface as the query sequence, then, the amino acid change and position are also indicated. Subsequently, the probability scores are computed, and the variant will either be classified as neutral or diseased. Similarly, the SIFT server requires the deposition of the protein sequence of interest and information on the substitutions to be analysed. In our study, the default settings of 3.0 for the median conservation score of sequences were unchanged. Once the query had been submitted, the SIFT server measured the tolerability versus intolerability of the substitutions based on the multiple alignment scores, location of the substitution and the physicochemical properties of the amino acid change. Finally, the Poly-Phen V2 gives the benign or pathogenic outcome based on the position of the substitution, and the interaction it makes in the secondary and tertiary conformations. The sequences are deposited on an online platform in FASTA format, and the location and type of the amino acid to be substituted are indicated on the user interface, with no further settings required. The results were then substantiated by the percentage sensitivity and specificity.

passages.text: tsRNA-3040b accumulates R-loop to regulate Trim35 transcription, which leads to disordered glycolysis and promotes PAECs proliferation
Background

Hypoxia significantly influences the development of pulmonary hypertension (PH). However, the role of transfer RNA-derived small RNAs (tsRNAs) produced by nuclease cleavage on PH, particularly their impact on the proliferation of pulmonary artery endothelial cells (PAECs), remains unclear.
Methods

To detect tsRNA expression, panoramic RNA display by overcoming RNA modification aborted sequencing (PANDORA-seq) sequencing analysis and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) were employed. The formation of R-loops between tsRNA and genomic DNA was confirmed through chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by polymerase chain reaction (ChIP-PCR) and Dot-blot analyses. Mouse PAECs and lung tissue were manipulated to either overexpress or inhibit tsRNA-3040b, followed by assessments of cell proliferation, RT-qPCR, and enzyme activity assays on three key glycolytic rate-limiting enzymes. Molecular docking, immunofluorescence and endogenous coprecipitation were used to demonstrate the colocalization of Trim35 and Wnt3a.
Results

The expression of tsRNA-Asp-GTC-3040b (termed tsRNA-3040b) was significantly increased in the lung tissue of a hypoxia-induced PH mouse model. By integrating database prediction with RNA sequencing, Trim35 was identified as a downstream target of tsRNA-3040b. ChIP-PCR and Dot-blot analyses using S9.6 indicated that tsRNA-3040b promoted R-loops in the genomic DNA of Trim35, thus inhibiting its transcription. Further investigation revealed that the Trim35 affected glucose metabolism levels through ubiquitinated substrate Wnt3a. Ultimately, it was elucidated that the tsRNA-3040b-Trim35-Wnt3a-glucose metabolism signaling pathway exacerbated the progression of PH.
Conclusions

This study highlights the role of tsRNA-3040b in promoting PH by influencing glucose metabolism processes. These results offer a new approach to treating PH and suggest that tsRNA-3040b could serve as a potential target for diagnosing PH and related conditions.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s11658-025-00816-5.
Background

Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a severe cardiovascular condition with various etiologies. The main pathological features of PH involve the smooth muscle layer proliferation, endothelial dysfunction, and adventitia fibrosis. PH can lead to right ventricular failure and death. In addition, PH is associated with metabolic pathway alterations, including abnormal glycolysis, glucose oxidation, and fatty acid oxidation. The dysfunction of pulmonary artery endothelial cells (PAECs) and glucose metabolism reprogramming may play a key role in the development of PH.

Transfer RNA-derived small RNA (tsRNA) is a type of noncoding RNA typically produced as a fragment following the cleavage of precursor or mature tRNA. It is categorized into tRF and tiRNA. Initially, tsRNAs were considered insignificant byproducts of tRNA degradation. However, recent studies have demonstrated that tsRNAs play roles in various biological processes, such as gene expression regulation, protein translation, cell proliferation, and DNA damage response. Moreover, tsRNAs have shown promise as therapeutic agents for conditions such as breast cancer, colorectal cancer, neurological diseases, and osteoporosis. Their role in influencing PAEC proliferation is still under investigation.

Glucose metabolism reprogramming is emerging as a critical regulator of endothelial cells. During the proliferation of endothelial cells, their energy primarily derived from ATP generated through glycolysis, resembling the Warburg effect seen in cancer cells. This metabolism pathway relies on glycolysis for energy production, bypassing the need for oxygen. Therefore, targeting glycolysis to inhibit ATP production in cancer cells is essential for controlling their growth. In addition, the enzymes involved in glycolysis have functions beyond energy production. For instance, hexokinase attached to mitochondria can affect mitochondrial dysfunction and cell death via BAX, while also playing a role in transcriptional regulation. PKM2 is impacted in the regulation of the biomacromolecules synthesis and tumor promotion through histone phosphorylation. Hexokinase, phosphofructokinase, and pyruvate kinase are key players in regulating carbohydrate metabolism. However, the specific mechanisms by which these enzymes and their metabolites function in the disease process of hypoxia-induced PH remain unclear.

During DNA repair and transcription, RNA forms R-loops, a hybrid structure. R-loops and other RNA-DNA hybrids play roles in DNA damage repair, transcription-replication conflicts (TRC), and chromophore rearrangement. Factors such as RNaseH enzymes, DNA:RNA helicase, and genome protection pathway proteins can prevent R-loop formation. The super enhancer circLrch3 can form R-loops with the host gene Lrch3 to regulate the apoptosis of pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (PASMCs), and finally promote the development of PH. Through Miranda sequencing, we identified Trim35 as a downstream target gene of tsRNA-3040b. Based on the unique structure of R-loops, we hypothesized that the triple-stranded nucleic acid structure could regulate the development of PH. This study examined the involvement of tsRNA-3040b in hypoxic-induced PH. Our results showed that tsRNA-3040b inhibited the transcription of its downstream target Trim35 by creating R-loops, leading to changes in the ubiquitination of Wnt3a, influencing the glycolytic metabolism of PAECs, and ultimately impacting the development of PH.
Methods
Cell culture

Mouse pulmonary artery endothelial cells (mPAECs) were purchased from Otwo Biotech (Cat# HTX3593, Shenzhen, China). They were cultured in Dulbecco's modified eagle medium (DMEM) medium containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FB25015, Clark, Australian) at 37  C in 5% CO2. Cells between passages 4 and 6 were used for experiments.
tsRNA transfection

The tsRNA-3040b mimic and inhibitor, along with the corresponding negative controls, were synthesized by RiboBio (Guanzhou, China). When mPAECs reached 60-70% confluency, the mimic (1 mug) or inhibitor (2 mug) was transfected into the cells using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen, USA) for 4-6 h according to the manufacturer's protocol. mPAECs were incubated for additional 24 h in fresh medium under normoxic and hypoxic (2% FiO2) conditions at 37  C. The transfected efficiency of tsRNA-3040b mimic and inhibitor was confirmed by RT-qPCR.
Plasmid overexpression and siRNA interference

The TRIM35 overexpression plasmid was synthesized by Genechem (Shanghai, China), and the WNT3A overexpression plasmid was synthesized by Miaoling Biotech (Wuhan, China). The siTrim35, siHK2, siPKM, siPFKM interference fragments, and negative controls were synthesized by Sanggon Biotech (Shanghai, China). mPAECs cells were inoculated into T-75 cell flasks and cultured for 24 h. Plasmids (2.5 mug) and interference fragments (2 mug) were transfected using Lipofectamine 2000 (0.5 mug/ml, Invitrogen, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions. mPAECs were incubated for additional 24 h in fresh medium under normoxic and hypoxic (2% FiO2) conditions at 37  C, and transfection efficiency was assessed using RT-qPCR and western blot analysis.
Western blot

Mouse tissue and cell samples were treated with cell lysis buffer (50 mM Tris, 150 mM NaCl, 1% deoxycholic acid, 0.1% SDS, and 0.5% Nonidet P-40) containing phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF). Samples (20 mug) were separated by 8-12% sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane and blocked with 5% nonfat dry milk in TBST (20 mM Tris, 150 mM NaCl, pH 7.6, 0.1% Tween 20) for 1-4 h. Membranes were incubated with primary antibodies (TRIM35 (1:1000, NOVUS, NBP2-88471), WNT3A (1:500, Cell Signaling, P56704), PCNA (1:1000, BOSTER, bm3888), and beta-actin (1:1000, Zhongshan JinQiao)) at 4  C overnight. The nitrocellulose membrane was washed with TBST the next day and incubated with appropriate secondary antibody in 5% skim milk at room temperature for 60 min. Membranes were then visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence kit (ECL, MA0186-1, Meilunbio, China) in a darkroom.
RNA extraction, reverse transcription, and quantitative RT-PCR

Total RNA from mPAECs and mouse lung tissues were extracted using TRizol (R0016, Beyotime, China). RNA (0.5 mug) was reverse-transcribed into cDNA using a reverse transcription kit (C10211-2, Beyotime, China). Real-time quantitative PCR was performed using SYBR Green (C10211-2, Beyotime, China) and LightCycler 480 system (Roche, Basel, Switzerland). Primers and other reagents for tsRNAs assays were purchased from RiboBio (MQP-0102; China). The fold increase relative to control samples was determined by the 2-DeltaDeltaCT method. U6 was used as an internal control for tsRNAs. beta-actin was used as internal control for mRNAs.
Dot blot

DNA (2 mug) was incubated with RNaseH (MCE, HY-KE7058) at 37  C for 1 h. Nitrocellulose membranes were soaked in phosphate buffered saline (PBS) and allowing to dry. The samples were then dropped onto dry nitrocellulose membranes, followed by 5 min crosslink using a UV crosslinker with a total dose of 66 kJ. The membranes were incubated in a 5% skim milk at ice bath on a shaker for 2 h. After washing with TBST, the membranes were incubated with primary antibody S9.6 (1:1000, GS50001, Mabnus) at 4  C overnight. The next day, the membranes were washed with TBST, incubated with secondary antibody in 5% skim milk, and developed using an ECL substrate solution (MA0186-1, Meilunbio, China).
Immunofluorescence staining

Cells were cultured on a round-bottom dish under normoxic and hypoxic conditions for 24 h, then washed three times with PBS for 5 min. The cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min, washed three times with PBS, and permeabilized with 0.3% Triton X-100 for 30 min. After additional washing with PBS, the cells were blocked with 3% bovine serum albumin (BSA) in PBS for 60 min, followed by incubation with primary antibody (1:100) at 4  C overnight. The next day, the cells were washed three times with PBS, incubated with fluorescent secondary antibody for 2 h at 37  C, and stained with DAPI (1:5000) for 10 min. The cells were then washed with PBS and observed under a fluorescence microscope.
EdU fluorescence experiment

Cells were cultured in a 24-well plate with round-bottom dish for 24 h. According to the experimental requirements, relevant treatments were performed, and the cells were labeled with 10 mumol/L EdU. The cells were incubated at 37  C for 2 h, then the medium was discarded, and 4% paraformaldehyde was added to fix the cells for 15 min. After discarding the fixation medium, the cells were washed with 3% BSA blocking solution and then incubated with 0.3% Triton X-100 for 15 min. Follow the kit instructions, the EdU working solution was prepared and added to the cells, which were incubated under light protection for 30 min. The medium was discarded, followed by the addition of the prepared Hoechst 33,342 solution and incubation for 10 min. Observations and analyses were performed using a live cell microscope (AF6000, Leica, Germany).
Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay

Cells were fixed with 1% paraformaldehyde for 10 min and neutralized with glycine. Cells were washed with precooled PBS, scraped, and centrifuged to obtain cell pellets. Subsequently, the cells were lysed for 30 min with a lysis buffer (140 mM NaCl, 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 1 mM EDTA, 0.5 mM EGTA, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS, 0.1% deoxycholate, 1 mM PMSF) containing protease inhibitors, and sonicated to produce chromatin fragments of predominantly ~200-400 base pairs (bp). Samples were centrifuged (12000 g, 4  C, 6 min), and the supernatant was mixed with 1.8 ml of dilution buffer; 40 muL was used for input. The diluted sample was mixed with 70 muL of Protein A + G agarose and rotated at 4  C for 30 min, then centrifuged to collect the supernatant, to which 2 mug of S9.6 antibody was added and rotated overnight at 4  C. The next day, 60 muL of Protein A + G agarose was added to the sample and rotated at 4  C for 60 min. Subsequently, the sample was centrifuged (1000 g, 4  C, 1 min) to collect the supernatant. The supernatant was washed sequentially with low-salt immune complex washing buffer, high-salt immune complex washing buffer, lithium chloride immune complex washing buffer, and TE buffer. After washing, new elution buffer was added for two washes, and the supernatant was collected in a new collection tube (final volume of 500 muL). The immunoprecipitate was incubated at 65  C (containing 20 muL of 5 M NaCl (1 muL added to Input)) for 4 h, then incubate at 10 muL 5 M EDTA with 20 muL 1 M Tris (pH 6.5) and 1 muL of 20 mg/mL proteinase K at 45  C for 1 h. Finally, genomic DNA was isolated using the DNA purification kit (Beyotime, China) and quantified by RT-qPCR.
Detection of glycolytic enzymes activity and ATP production

After modeling the PAECs and scraping the cells to obtain cell pellets, corresponding extraction solutions were added, and the cells were subjected to ultrasonic disruption. Activities of hexokinase, fructokinase and pyruvate kinase activities were detected by the corresponding enzyme activity kit (Nanjing Jiancheng, China). The production of pyruvate, ATP, and lactate were measured by the corresponding assay kit (Nanjing Jiancheng, China).
Co-immunoprecipitation

mPAECs were cultured in 100 mm dishes at a density of 1 x 106 cells/dish for 24 h. The culture medium was discarded, and the cells were lysed with a cell lysis buffer (200 muL/106 cells) containing PMSF, followed by centrifugation (13,500 rpm, 4  C, 10 min) to collect the supernatant. The supernatant was then subjected to immunoprecipitation using TRIM35 antibody (1 mug). Subsequently, the expression of WNT3A and ubiquitination levels were analyzed by western blotting and ubiquitin-specific antibodies.
In situ hybridization

After culturing the cells for 24 h, and the cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min. After discarding the fixation medium, the cells were stained with the tsRNA-3040b probe (1 muM) in hybridization solution overnight at 4  C to determine the localization of tsRNA-3040b. Finally, the nuclei were stained with prepared DAPI, and the images were observed under a fluorescence microscope (Nikon, Japan).
Animal models

The tsRNA-3040b agomir (double chain, tsRNAs mimics undergone special chemical modifications) and antagomir (single chain, tsRNAs inhibitor undergone special chemical modifications, strongly competing with mature tsRNAs) viruses of tsRNA-3040b were synthesized by GENEWIZ (Suzhou, China). Compared with mimics and inhibitors, agomir and antagomir have higher affinity and stability with cell membranes, making them particularly suitable for in vivo animal experiments. Divide the mice into four group: normoxic, normoxic plus tsRNA-3040b agomir, hypoxic, and hypoxic plus tsRNA-3040b antagomir (C57BL, equal number of males and females, six per group). Mice were anesthetized with trichloroethanol (approximately 200-250 mg/kg, intraperitoneal injection). The viral titer was calculated by mouse body weight, intravenous injection was administered to generate tsRNA-3040b lentiviral model mice, and after 1-week of stabilization under normoxic conditions, the mice were subjected to normoxic (FiO2: 21%) or hypoxic (FiO2: 10%) conditions for 21 days. Echocardiography was conducted in small animals using the Vevo 2100 imaging system to obtain the PA velocity time integral, PA acceleration time, and PA ejection time. Thereafter, right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) was measured with a Millar catheter (Millar Instruments, Inc., Houston, Texas) inserted through the right jugular vein. The aortae, carotid arteries, liver, spleen, and kidney tissues were then isolated to extract RNA for tissue specificity analysis. In addition, lung tissue, heart, and right ventricle tissues were isolated to extract total RNA and proteins, and tsRNA-3040b levels were detected by RT-qPCR.
Seahorse assay

mPAECs was seeded into an XFe-24 well plate at a density of 1 x 104 cells per 250 microL/well. Transfection was performed after the cells were attached. On the assay day, media in the wells was replaced with Seahorse DMEM medium (supplemented with 1 mM pyruvate, 2 mM glutamine, and 10 mM glucose) for the mito stress test. The glycolysis stress test included only 2 mM glutamine. Cells were washed once and equilibrated in a non-CO2 incubator for 50 min. These tests measured oxygen consumption rates (OCR) and extracellular acidifcation rates (ECAR) using the Seahorse XFe-24 analyzer. In the mito stress test, cells were treated with 1.5 microM oligomycin, followed by 0.25 microM FCCP, and then 1 microM rotenone and antimycin A. The glycolysis stress test involved treating cells with 10 mM glucose, 1.5 microM oligomycin, and 50 mM 2-deoxy-d-glucose. The experiment was repeated five times.
Data analysis

Data are expressed as mean +- SEM. Experiments were repeated at least three times. Comparisons between two groups were performed using unpaired two-tailed t-tests, while comparisons among multiple groups were carried out using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). All statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism 8.0, with exactly P values indicated in the figure legends. P values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.
Results
Increased levels of tsRNA-3040b in hypoxic pulmonary hypertension

Expression level of tsRNA-3040b was increased in hypoxic PH. mPAECs were exposed to normoxia or hypoxia for 24 h, and PANDORA sequencing was performed. A The left shows small noncoding RNAs of different lengths (nucleotide, nt), the upper right shows the alignment success rate for rRNA-derived sncRNAs, the lower right panel displayed the proportion of tsRNAs from different sources. B The radar chart illustrates the proportion of different types of tsRNA under hypoxic conditions. The polygons of different colors in the chart represent the abundance distribution of tsRNA in different groups (black represents the normoxic group, and red represents the hypoxic group). Each axis corresponds to a tsRNA subtype (such as tRNA origin). The length of the axis indicates the relative expression level of that subtype, and the larger the polygon area, the higher the overall tsRNA diversity or expression level. C Volcanic plots show significantly altered expression of tsRNAs. D Cluster heatmap of the identified 18 upregulated and 9 downregulated tsRNAs. E RT-qPCR detects the level of tsRNA-3040b in mPAECs after exposure to normoxic and hypoxic conditions for 24 h (n = 3). U6 was used as a reference gene. F RT-qPCR verifies the transcriptional level of tsRNA-3040b in hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension mouse lung tissue (n = 4). U6 was used as reference gene. G Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis shows the distribution of tsRNA-3040b in mPAECs under normoxic and hypoxic conditions. U6 and 18S probes serve as positive markers for the nucleus and cytoplasm. Data are presented as mean +- SEM. Unpaired two-tailed t-tests were used for comparisons. Hyp, hypoxia; miRNA, microRNA; Nor, normoxia; piRNA, PIWI-interacting RNA; rRNA MG, rRNA map genome; rRNA UMG, rRNA un map genome; rsRNA, ribosomal RNA-derived Small RNA; sncRNA, small noncoding RNA; tsRNA, transfer RNA-derived small RNA; Unanno MG, Unanno map genome; Unanno UMG, Unanno un map genome

We performed PANDORA sequencing on mPAECs under normoxic and hypoxic conditions, identifying significantly altered sncRNAs including miRNAs, piRNAs, rsRNAs, and tsRNAs in hypoxia. Our study focused on tsRNAs with lengths of 15-45 nucleotide (nt) (Fig. 1a, left). The pie chart illustrates a 78.9% alignment success rate for rRNA-derived sncRNAs (Fig. 1a, upper right), confirming data reliability, while the lower right panel displayed the proportion of tsRNAs from different sources. Radar chart analysis revealed that the hypoxic group (red) exhibited larger polygon areas compared with the normoxic group (black), indicating significantly increased tsRNA diversity and expression levels under hypoxia (Fig. 1b). Using thresholds of P < 0.05 and log2FC > 2, volcano plot analysis and cluster heatmap identified 18 upregulated and 9 downregulated tsRNAs under hypoxia (Fig. 1c, d). Following qPCR validation, we found six significantly differentially expressed tsRNAs (Supplementary Fig. S1), with this study particular focusing on tsRNA-Asp-GTC-3040b (tsRNA-3040b). Given that hypoxia plays crucial role in pulmonary hypertension development, we cultured mPAECs under 3% FiO2 for 24 h, and established a hypoxia (10% FiO2)-induced PH mouse model. RT-qPCR analysis demonstrated significantly elevated tsRNA-3040b levels in hypoxic mPAECs and mouse lung tissues (Fig. 1e, f). In situ hybridization further revealed nuclear accumulation of tsRNA-3040b under hypoxic conditions (Fig. 1g).
Regulation of glycolysis and proliferation by tsRNA-3040b in mPAECs

tsRNA-3040b regulates mPAECs glycolysis. A A cartoon showed the sequences of tRNA-Asp-GTC, tsRNA-3040b, tsRNA-3040b mimics, and the tsRNA-3040b inhibitors. B RT-qPCR detects the level of tsRNA-3040b. mPAECs were transfected with the tsRNA-3040b mimic or inhibitor for 4-6 h. Cells were incubated for additional 24 h in fresh medium under normaxic and hypoxic conditions at 37  C. U6 was used as a reference gene. n = 4/group. C RT-qPCR detects glycolytic kinase Hk2 mRNA levels (n = 6). beta-actin was used as reference gene. D HK2 enzyme activity assay (n = 7). E The extracellular acidifcation rates (ECAR) involved treating cells with 10 mM glucose, 1.5 microM oligomycin, and 50 mM 2-deoxy-D-glucose. F, G Glycolysis and glycolytic reserve were measured (n = 5). H The oxygen consumption rates (OCR) involved treating cells with 1.5 microM oligomycin, followed by 0.25 microM FCCP, and then 1 microM rotenone and antimycin A. I-J ATP production and maximal respiration were calculated (n = 5). K-M The production of pyruvate, ATP, and lactate were measured by the corresponding assay kit (n = 4). Data are presented as mean +- SEM. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was employed for comparisons. Hyp, hypoxia; Inh, tsRNA-3040b inhibitor; mimics, tsRNA-3040b mimic; NC, negative controls; Nor, normoxia

Glycolysis is the primary process by which cells generate ATP to provide energy under anaerobic conditions. In our previously study, we found glycolysis, glycolytic capacity, and glycolytic reserve were significantly induced by hypoxia in PAECs. To investigate whether tsRNA-3040b influences glycolysis in PH, we either overexpressed or inhibited tsRNA-3040b expression in mPAECs using mimics and inhibitors (Fig. 2a lower panel, Fig. 2b). After hypoxic treatment, RT-qPCR and enzyme activity assays were performed on three key glycolytic enzymes. The results indicated that hypoxia elevated hexokinase expression levels and activities, but this increase was diminished when tsRNA-3040b was inhibited (Fig. 2c, d). Similar trends were observed for the expression and activities of pyruvate kinase and fructose phosphate kinase, supporting our hypothesis that tsRNA-3040b influences glycolysis in PAECs (Supplementary Fig. S2a-d). In order to examine whether the TCA cycle is regulated by tsRNA-3040b, Seahorse technology was used to detect the metabolic characteristics of mPAECs under normoxic and hypoxic conditions. ECAR analysis showed that overexpression of tsRNA-3040b under normoxic conditions significantly increased glycolysis related indicators (glycolysis, glycolic capacity, and glycolic reserve). Knocking down tsRNA-3040b under hypoxic conditions can restore glycolysis levels to normoxic state, indicating that tsRNA-3040b affects PAECs function by regulating glycolysis (Fig. 2e-g, Supplementary Fig. S2e). The OCR experiment found that hypoxia significantly reduced OCR and ATP production, but overexpression of tsRNA-3040b had no significant effect on ATP production (slightly increased under normoxia and slightly decreased under hypoxia) and mitochondrial functional parameters (maximal respiration, spare capacity) (Fig. 2h-j, Supplementary Fig. S2f). In addition, the accumulation of key glycolysis products, pyruvic acid and lactic acid, decreased with the addition of the tsRNA-3040b inhibitor in hypoxic mPAECs (Fig. 2k, l). During glycolysis, ATP is generated to supply energy, and ATP levels rose under hypoxic conditions but dropped with the introduction of the tsRNA-3040b inhibitor, suggesting that tsRNA-3040b inhibitor reduces glycolytic capacity (Fig. 2m).

tsRNA-3040b modulates glycolysis in mPAECs and impacts their proliferation. A, B Representative images and summarized data of EdU staining and Ki67 staining in mPAECs. mPAECs were transfected with tsRNA-3040b mimic, or tsRNA-3040b inhibitor, or negative control and then exposed to normoxia or hypoxia for 24 h, with the nuclei stained with Hoechst or DAPI (blue). C Western blot analysis detected the PCNA expression (n = 3). beta-actin was used as an internal reference. D Tubule formation assays. E RT-qPCR verified the interference efficiency of siRNAs targeted to Hk2 (n = 4). F, G Western blot analysis detected the expression of HK2 after treatment with siRNA or tsRNA-3040b mimic (n = 6). H, I Representative images and summarized data of EdU staining and Ki67 staining in mPAECs. mPAECs were transfected with tsRNA-3040b mimic, and treated with siHK2, siPFKM, or siPKM under normoxic conditions, with the nuclei stained with Hoechst or DAPI (blue) (n = 5). Data are presented as mean +- SEM. One-way ANOVA was employed for comparisons. HK, hexokinase; Hyp, hypoxia; Inh, tsRNA-3040b inhibitor; mimics, tsRNA-3040b mimic; NC, negative controls; Nor, normoxia; PFKM, phosphofructokinase, muscle; PKM, pyruvate kinase M1/2

In PH, endothelial cells are damaged and exhibit increased proliferation. We investigated the role of tsRNA-3040b in PH by assessing mPAECs proliferation and tubule formation. The tsRNA-3040b mimic promoted cell proliferation, as evidenced by EdU and Ki67 immunofluorescence (Fig. 3a, b). Transfection with the tsRNA-3040b mimic also increased the proliferation marker PCNA compared with the control group, and this increase was significantly lowered under hypoxic conditions following tsRNA-3040b inhibition (Fig. 3c). Overexpression of tsRNA-3040b also significantly enhanced the tubule formation ability of mPAECs (Fig. 3d). Considering tsRNA-3040b's impacts on glycolysis and ATP production, we further investigated whether tsRNA-3040b influences cell proliferation through glycolysis. Hexokinase (HK), fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase (PFKM), and pyruvate kinase (PKM) are three key glycolytic enzymes in PAECs that responded to hypoxia. We knocked down three enzymes using designed siRNA; the knockdown efficiency was confirmed by RT-qPCR and western blot, with the best knockdown siRNA segment selected for for following experiment (Fig. 3e, f, and Supplementary Fig. S3a-d). The siRNA was able to prevent the increased HK, PFKM, and PKM expression induced by tsRNA-3040b mimic (Fig. 3g, Supplementary Fig. 3e, f). EdU and Ki67 immunofluorescence results revealed enhanced cell proliferation following the introduction of the tsRNA-3040b mimic. This proliferative effect was reversed when each of the three glycolysis kinases was individually interfered with, confirming that glycolysis in PH affects mPAECs proliferation (Fig. 3h, i). These findings provide preliminary evidence that tsRNA-3040b may regulate PAECs proliferation by modulating glycolysis enzymes.

To investigate the role of tsRNA-3040b in the development of hypoxia-induced PH model, 8-week-old C57 mice were injected with agomir and antagomir viruses via the tail vein and then exposed to hypoxia for 3 weeks to induce a hypoxic PH mouse model (Fig. 4a). The ultrasound examination confirmed that cardiac function deteriorated under hypoxia. This was restored with tsRNA-3040b inhibition (Fig. 4b). In addition, right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) measurements indicated a significant pressure increase during hypoxia, which markedly improved after tsRNA-3040b inhibition (Fig. 4c). Immunofluorescence using the endothelial cell marker CD31 indicated that hypoxia stimulated angiogenesis (Fig. 4d). H and E staining revealed that the tsRNA-3040b inhibitor reduced vascular remodeling in lung tissue (Fig. 4e). Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) experiments of the patients with iPAH showed increased expression of tsRNA-3040b (Fig. 4f). FISH experiments of the carotid artery showed no significant differences in tsRNA-3040b expression (Fig. 4g). However, FISH of lung tissue revealed increased tsRNA-3040b expression under hypoxic conditions (Fig. 4h). Similar results were observed in the lung tissue of patients with PH (Fig. 4i). To explore whether tsRNA-3040b affects glycolysis levels, we performed similar tests in animal models. RT-qPCR analysis indicated that tsRNA-3040b antagomir significantly reduced hexokinase expression and activity in the lung tissues of hypoxic mice (Fig. 4i, j). We also measured fructose phosphate kinase and pyruvate kinase expression and activities using RT-qPCR and activity assays, finding that tsRNA-3040b agomir administration enhanced glycolysis (Supplementary Fig. S4a-d). Consistent results were observed when measuring lactate acid content (Fig. 4k). Western blot analysis showed elevated PCNA protein expression (Fig. 4l) following tsRNA-3040b agomir treatment, and immunofluorescence indicated reduced Ki67 expression (Fig. 4m) after tsRNA-3040b antagomir application. These results suggest that tsRNA-3040b promotes glycolysis and PAECs proliferation in vivo, subsequently influencing the progression of PH.

Given that tsRNA-3040b accumulates in the nucleus of mPAECs under hypoxic conditions (Fig. 1g), we proposed that tsRNA-3040b might have a role in gene transcription regulation. After intersecting the complementary genes of tsRNA-3040b in the Miranda database with the significantly altered dataset of hypoxic PAECs, we screened 16 downregulated genes and 13 upregulated genes (Supplementary Fig. S5). Referring to the literature, Trim35 was found to be a gene related to glucose metabolism. Cluster heatmap and volcano plot analysis also revealed that Trim35, which is known to be downregulated under hypoxic conditions, is a candidate gene of tsRNA-3040b (Fig. 5a, b). Subsequent RT-qPCR and western blot analyses confirmed that Trim35 mRNA and protein levels were decreased under hypoxia (Fig. 5c, d). Transfecting mPAECs with a tsRNA-3040b mimics decreased Trim35 under normoxia, while tsRNA-3040b inhibitor led to increased Trim35 transcription and protein levels under hypoxic conditions (Fig. 5e, f). In the PH lung tissue, TRIM35 expression was significantly downregulated by tsRNA-3040b agomir or hypoxia at both transcriptional and protein levels, while the tsRNA-3040b antagomir restored the Trim35 expression under hypoxia conditions (Fig. 5g, h).

The presence of R-loop peak on Trim35 gene was predicted through the R-loop database (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/databasecommons/database/id/1809). Next, Dot blotting analysis with the R-loops marker S9.6 showed that overexpression of tsRNA-3040b by mimics or hypoxia enhances R-loop formation, while knockdown of tsRNA-3040b weakens R-loop formation under hypoxic conditions. Moreover, the addition of R-loop inhibitor RNase H eliminates all of these effects (Fig. 5i). The inhibition of Trim35 expression induced by tsRNA-3040b mimics was prevented after RNase H treatment (Fig. 5j), confirming that tsRNA-3040b affects Trim35 transcription through the R-loop. In hypoxia, S9.6 nuclear staining in mPAECs increased under hypoxia, which was prevented by the tsRNA-3040b inhibitor (Fig. 5k). Furthermore, ChIP-PCR with S9.6 antibody confirmed the specific R-loop site on the Trim35 gene, the promoter region from -431 to -44, as well as the coding region at +106 to +400, and +488 to +508 (Fig. 5l), and also increased tsRNA-3040b in the R-loop structure during hypoxia (Fig. 5m). These findings preliminarily support the hypothesis that tsRNA-3040b may promote or stabilize the R-loop structure in the promoter region and coding region of Trim35, thereby inhibiting its transcription (Fig. 5n).

The ubiquitin-proteasome system is the primary pathway for protein degradation, which not only controls protein quantity but also their activity, interactions, and subcellular localization through various forms of ubiquitin chains such as mono-ubiquitination and polyubiquitination. This system plays a pivotal role in physiological processes including cell proliferation, apoptosis, autophagy, endocytosis, DNA damage repair, and immune response. Trim35 acts as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, facilitating ubiquitination. The function of Trim35 ubiquitination targets was evaluated. We first evaluated the knockdown of Trim35 by siRNAs by using RT-qPCR (Fig. 6a). Interaction factors for Trim35 were identified using the prediction tool on www.ubibrowser.com, with Wnt3a emerging as a significant factor. Gene Ontology (GO) analysis revealed that Wnt3a regulates glycolysis and is crucial in this process. Western blot assays confirmed that Wnt3a protein expression increased under hypoxic conditions in mPAECs and mouse lung tissue (Fig. 6b, c). After Trim35 knockdown with si-Trim35, Wnt3a protein expression was restored (Fig. 6d). Molecular docking showed their spatial interactions (Fig. 6e). Immunofluorescence and endogenous coprecipitation of mPAECs lysates provided further evidence of their colocalization (Fig. 6f). Experiments indicated that ubiquitination levels decreased when si-Trim35 was applied (Fig. 6g). In addition, Wnt3A protein expression was restored with the proteasome inhibitor MG-132 (Fig. 6h). To examine changes in glycolysis following Trim35 modulation, RT-qPCR and hexokinase activity assessments were conducted, showing increased glycolysis with Trim35 disruption and decreased glycolysis with Trim35 overexpression (Fig. 6i, j). Validation of pyruvate kinase and phosphofructokinase confirmed these findings (Supplementary Fig. S6a-d). Measurement of glycolysis products revealed decreased pyruvate, lactate levels, and ATP production after Trim35 overexpression (Fig. 6k, m), indicating that Trim35 inhibits glycolysis by ubiquintinating and degrading Wnt3a.

In order to confirm the tsRNA-3040b/Trim35 modulated glycolysis through Wnt3a, rescue experiments were performed. RT-qPCR and hexokinase assays revealed a reduction in hexokinase levels with Trim35 overexpression, whereas co-overexpression of Wnt3a restored hexokinase transcription and enzyme activity (Fig. 7a, b). Further RT-qPCR analysis and enzymatic activity measurements of phosphofructokinase and pyruvate kinase corroborated these findings (Supplementary Fig. S7a-d). Measurements of pyruvate and lactic acid, the end products of glycolysis, after Wnt3a overexpression showed elevated levels, leading to increased ATP production (Fig. 7c-e). PCNA expression indicated a significant increase in cell proliferation following Wnt3a overexpression (Fig. 7f). Ki67 immunofluorescence and EdU assays analyses confirmed that Wnt3a promotes cell proliferation, which is counteracted by Trim35 overexpression, indicating that the Wnt3a meditated glycolysis is inhibited by the ubiquitination activity of Trim35 (Fig. 7g, h). These findings suggest that Trim35 lead to the downregulation of Wnt3a through the ubiquitination under normoxic conditions, when PAECs exposure to hypoxia, the increasing generation of tsRNA-3040b suppresses Trim35 transcription by promoting R-loop formation in the Trim35 gene, leading to the increasing expression of Wnt3a, which activities the glycolysis enzymes and stimulates PAECs proliferation (Fig. 8).
Discussion

In this study, we investigated the localization and function of a novel tsRNA, designated tsRNA-3040b in PH. This molecule was observed to be upregulated in hypoxic mouse PAECs and lung tissue, with its overexpression resulting in increased cell proliferation. To investigate the similarity between the excessive proliferation of PAECs in PH and the Warburg effect seen in tumor cells, we assessed the expression of key glycolytic enzymes. Our findings revealed that glycolysis levels increased in hypoxic PH. In addition, ATP levels in PAECs were found to be elevated, but significantly dropped upon the inhibition of tsRNA-3040b during hypoxia, indicating that the excessive proliferation of PAECs is driven by glycolysis. The examination of cell proliferation after targeting three enzymes supported our hypothesis.

To further explore how tsRNA-3040b influences glycolysis, we identified Wnt3a as a downstream target that plays a crucial role in the anaerobic glycolysis of tumor cells. We experimentally demonstrated that the upregulation of tsRNA-3040b under hypoxic conditions boosts PAEC glycolysis by raising Wnt3a levels. However, our investigations revealed that Wnt3a is not directly controlled by tsRNA-3040b. To elucidate the connection between these elements, we demonstrated that hypoxia prompts the accumulation of tsRNA-3040b within the nucleus. This accumulation decreases Trim35 mRNA levels by promoting R-loop structure in Trim35 during transcription, ultimately resulting in a reduction of Trim35 protein levels.

Our study has uncovered a novel type of tsRNA, tsRNA-3040b, in the context of PH. This tsRNA inhibits the transcription of Trim35 by promoting R-loop formation in Trim35 DNA in the nucleus, consequently mitigating Wnt3a degradation via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. This mechanism elevates the levels of key enzymes involved in glycolysis, boosts the glycolytic activity of PAECs under hypoxic conditions, and ultimately drives excessive cell proliferation. Initially regarded as mere by-products of tRNA degradation upon their discovery, tsRNAs have since been recognized for their functional roles following cleavage of mature tRNAs by the Dicer enzyme and angiopoietin ANG, leading to the generation of small tsRNA fragments.

Recent advances in high-throughput sequencing have facilitated the investigation of various biological roles of tsRNA. These functions include inhibiting apoptosis, regulating epigenetics, and promoting cell proliferation. Research has demonstrated that tsRNA can both promote and inhibit cancer development, as well as other diseases. In addition, tsRNAs have been found to effectively inhibit ocular angiogenesis. They play a role in breast cancer by upregulating expression and inducing cell proliferation. In chronic lymphocytic leukemia and lung cancer, ts46 and ts47 function and act as tumor suppressors. Furthermore, tRF-Glu-TTC-027 decreases the incidence and progression of bone cancer by inhibiting the MAPK signaling pathway, while tRF-Gln-TTG-006 promotes the migration of hepatocellular carcinoma stem cells by inhibiting NDFIP2 and activating the AKT signaling pathway.

The intricate causes of pulmonary hypertension (PH) have led to the development of various treatment approaches in recent years, with several tsRNA subtypes gaining significant interest. In our study, we identified tsRNA-3040b which appears to exert a therapeutic effect on PH. Our experimental data strongly support this observation. In a mouse model of hypoxia-induced PH, the application of the tsRNA-3040b resulted in several beneficial outcomes: an increase in pulmonary artery acceleration time, a decrease in RVSP, and a reduction in pulmonary fibrosis. These findings suggest that tsRNA-3040b holds considerable potential for clinical application value and may emerge as a novel treatment option for PH.

Recent strategies aimed at restoring normal glucose oxidation have shown promise in treating PH, emphasizing the critical role of metabolic abnormalities in the disease's progression. In this condition, cellular metabolism becomes abnormal, leading cells to rely more on anaerobic respiration rather than mitochondrial respiration. This state is marked by elevated glycolytic activity rather than issues primarily related to mitochondrial respiration. In recent years, the methods aimed at normalizing glucose oxidation have shown potential for treating PH, underscoring the significant role of this metabolic abnormality in the disease's progression. Recent investigations suggest that restoring normal glycolytic levels in PAECs could represent a new therapeutic avenue for PH. This study sough to determine whether tsRNA-3040b promotes PAECs proliferation by influencing glycolysis, a crucial pathway for cellular energy production in PH. To evaluate this hypothesis, we conducted a series of experiments at both cellular and animal levels. The results revealed a significant increase in the levels of glycolysis-related kinases under hypoxic conditions. Conversely, the knockdown of tsRNA-3040b led to a marked reduction in glycolysis levels. These results unequivocally demonstrate that tsRNA-3040b facilitates glycolysis during the pathological process of PH.

Cancer cells exhibit numerous characteristics, with their unlimited proliferation being a primary defining trait. The glycolysis pathway is a crucial component in glucose metabolism, operating in both aerobic and anaerobic environments, serving as the shared metabolic pathway for glucose breakdown under both conditions. The glycolysis that occurs in the presence of oxygen is referred to as the "Warburg effect."; under hypoxic conditions, the conversion of pyruvate to lactic acid is an integral part of glycolysis. Cell proliferation is essential for living organisms, with eukaryotic cells primarily undergoing mitosis. Increased glycolysis levels are a significant metabolic feature of tumor cells, crucial for their proliferation by providing the energy and metabolites necessary for tumor growth. In addition, glycolysis plays an essential role in the occurrence and development of cancer. During the proliferation of tumor cells, glycolysis, although it generates relatively little energy overall, has the advantage of providing energy quickly. This rapid energy production supports cell growth in a short period of time. Recent studies have shown that glycolysis plays a crucial role in tumor development, impacting tumor proliferation, angiogenesis, and lymphogenesis, and is correlated with tumor prognosis. In PH, the abnormal PAECs proliferation is closely associated with glycolytic dysregulation. In our study, tsRNA-3040b inhibitors were shown to lower pyruvate and lactate levels, disrupt redox balance in the cells, and reduce ATP synthesis. This decline in metabolic activity within PAECs results in diminished energy availability, ultimately leading to reduced proliferation of these cells. In summary, tsRNA-3040b increases glycolysis in PAECs, thereby promoting cell proliferation and impacting the progression of PH.

The transcriptional activity can lead to the generation of R-loops. Studies have shown that in genes transcribed by RNA polymerase II, R-loops predominantly form at the promoter, the initiation site of transcription, and the termination region. The transcriptional process mediated by RNA polymerase II results in an accumulation of R-loops. In the 5' region of 18S, the increase in R-loop is associated with RNA polymerase I activity. RNA polymerase III generates R-loops during the transcription of 5S rRNA genes. Conversely R-loops associated with tRNA genes, which are also transcribed by RNA polymerase III, only occur when RNase H is dysfunctional. Our findings indicate a decrease in S9.6 expression following RNaseH addition, implying a reduction in R-loop formation. Moreover, our data reveal that tsRNA-3040b affects both the protein and transcription levels of Trim35. We have experimentally demonstrated that tsRNA-3040b can increase R-loops between the promoter and coding region of Trim35. In PAECs, overexpression of tsRNA-3040b restored transcriptional silencing of Trim35, resulting in transcriptional abnormalities and reduced Trim35 transcriptional levels, an effect that was alleviated by tsRNA-3040b inhibitors. We present the evidences of R-loops formation with tsRNA-3040b and with Trim35. However, owing to the short length of tsRNA-3040b, its ChIRP probe could not be successfully synthesized, so the experiment of using Trim35 promoter and coding sequence primer amplification after pulling down DNA with tsRNA-3040b probe was not realized to directly prove tsRNA-3040b localization in the R-loop, we suggested that tsRNA-3040b may promote or stabilize the R-loop structure of its target gene Trim35 by binding to a specific region, thereby inhibiting its transcription. Furthermore, R-loops are induced in more genes and are not specific to TRIM35 during hypoxic conditions. Our recent study indicated that R-loop formation in FOXP1 genes regulated the level of FOXP1 protein and participated in the proliferation of PASMCs during the development of PH. Global analyses should be conducted in future studies to better understand the landscape of R-loops and their roles across different genes, which could represent a novel therapeutic approach for PH.

Ubiquitination is a key post-translational modification that regulates cellular protein levels by attaching ubiquitin molecules to target proteins, marking them for degradation via the proteasome. The main steps involve transferring the activated ubiquitin molecule from the ubiquitin-activating enzyme E1 to the E2 enzyme, linking the E2-bound ubiquitin to the target protein via the ubiquitin ligase E3, and forming a small ubiquitin molecular chain at the end of the labeled protein molecule. This chain is then specifically recognized and degraded by the 26 s proteasome. Currently, E3 ubiquitin ligases are recognized as the most impactful ubiquitin enzymes owing to their ability to selectively recruit substrate proteins for ubiquitination. In addition, E3 ubiquitin ligases play a vital role in cancer by regulating the cell cycle to promote cell growth. The TRIM family, a type of zinc finger structure found in E3 ubiquitin ligases, can operate as monomers or homodimers independently of other proteins. TRIM proteins are involved in various biological processes, including cell proliferation and transcriptional regulation. TRIM35 contributes to cancer by inhibiting cell activity in hepatocellular carcinoma through blocking PKM2 Y105 phosphorylation; and severs as a tumor suppressor in breast cancer by inhibiting cell growth and promoting programmed cell death. We examined the role of TRIM35 in glycolysis related to PH. Our experimental results indicate that elevated TRIM35 expression under hypoxic conditions may reduce glycolytic activity; however, the role of ubiquitination in this process remains unclear. Consequently, we sought to explore the relationship between elevated glycolytic levels and TRIM35 self-ubiquitination. In screening for TRIM35 ubiquitinated substrate, we focused on WNT3A, a member of the Wnt protein family. Our experimental data confirmed the interaction between WNT3A and TRIM35, highlighting its functional significance. The Wnt family comprises a diverse group of secreted proteins, with 19 identified in humans. WNT3A is extensively expressed and is crucial for regulating cell functions such as proliferation and differentiation. Research indicates that WNT3A enhances glucose metabolism in cortical neurons by stimulating glycolysis to support energy requirements; it facilitates the phosphorylation of PFKP at S386, resulting in increased PFKP expression, which promotes cell proliferation and aids in cancer cell migration. Our study, along with previous studies, demonstrates that tsRNA-3040b elevates glycolysis in PH by influencing the TRIM35-mediated ubiquitination of WNT3A, which in turn enhances PAECs proliferation.

The limitations of this study include: (i) the unproven effects of other significantly upregulated or downregulated tsRNAs on glycolysis; (ii) beside the promotion of R-loop formation, other established tsRNA mechanisms, such as inhibition of mRNA translation, promotion of ribosome biogenesis, and regulation of other epigenetic processes including DNA methylation could not excluded; and since only a 24-h hypoxia window was selected because this duration is commonly used to capture stable changes in our readouts (e.g. proliferation and cell cycle progression), future work using inducible perturbations and shorter hypoxia windows (e.g., 2-6 h) will more directly address immediate signaling events of tsRNAs; (iii) the exclusive use of the hypoxic PH model; and (iv) the absence of virus targeting PAECs.
Conclusions

From our findings, it is evident that tsRNA-3040b and Trim35 are pivotal in PH progression. Regulating the levels of tsRNA-3040b or inhibiting its interaction with Trim35 could potentially control PH development. Furthermore, our data reveal that Wnt3a enhances glycolysis and promote PAEC proliferation. It is highly probable that inhibitor targeting tsRNA-3040b could emerge as a novel therapeutic strategy for PH.

passages.text: The significance of endocannabinoid receptors and endocannabinoids in the lower urinary and genital tract
Purpose

The cannabinoid receptor (CB) signal transduction is a complex system that is relatively widespread in mammalian cells and tissues. By regulating the local levels and actions of other chemical signals, it can activate multiple cascades in different organs. Cannabinoid receptors and endocannabinoids are also present in the human lower urinary tract (LUT) and genital tract, including the urinary bladder, prostate, urethra, penile erectile tissue and seminal vesicles. The present review aims to give an overview on what has emerged from basic research and clinical approaches on the role of the endocannabinoid system (ECS) in the human lower urinary tract and reproductive tissues.
Methods

This review article highlights some key data from research into the cannabinoid system and its potential role in the control of micturition, reproductive functions and also dysfunctions of the lower urinary tract.

annotations.text: dysfunctions of the lower urinary tract

passages.text: Results

While basic research findings on the ECS in reproductive tissues (penile erectile tissue, seminal vesicles) have not yet been supplemented by data from trials addressing clinical conditions such as erectile dysfunction (ED) and ejaculatory disorders (for example, premature ejaculation), targeting the ECS has been suggested as a pharmacological approach to treat disorders of bladder filling and storage functions.

infons.name: Congenital Hereditary and Neonatal Diseases and Abnormalities

annotations.text: disorders of bladder filling and storage functions

passages.text: Conclusion

Despite some preclinical data may favor a role of receptors, ligands and regulatory proteins of the ECS in the LUT, additional clinical evidence is required in order to support a significance of a modulation of the pathways stimulated by cannabinoid molecules in the treatment of dysfunctions of the lower urinary and genital tract.

annotations.text: dysfunctions of the lower urinary and genital tract

passages.text: Introduction

In the previous decades since its discovery, the pleiotropic endogenous cannabinoid system (ECS) has been implicated to trigger many physiological processes, and the signaling pathways mediating many of these responses, particularly in the central nervous system, have come into light. It has become obvious that the cannabinoid receptor signal transduction is a complex system that is relatively widespread in mammalian tissues and cells and can activate, by regulating the local levels and actions of other chemical signals, multiple cascades in different organs including those of the lower urinary and genital tract of humans. This system comprises of at least two G-protein-coupled receptors, known as the cannabinoid receptors CB1 and CB2, and endogenous agonists of these receptors, known as endocannabinoids, of which anandamide (N-arachidonoyl ethanolamide = AEA), 2-arachidonoyl glycerol (2-AG), palmitoyl ethanolamide (PEA) and oleoyl ethanolamide (OEA) are the most important. AEA is known to attach with higher affinity to the CB1 receptor [HS, IM]. OEA and PEA mainly act as entourage compounds by inhibiting the hydrolysis of AEA by the enzyme fatty acid amide hydrolase FAAH [HS]. The non-endogenous cannabinoid delta9-tetrahydrocannabinol (Delta9-THC) is the major psychoactive constituent of the plant Cannabis sativa and is characterized by a partial agonist activity at the cannabinoid receptor CB1, located mainly in the central nervous system. FAAH hydrolyzes anandamide into arachidonic acid and ethanolamine while monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL) hydrolyzes 2-AG to arachidonic acid and glycerol, thus facilitating regulation of the levels of endocannabinoids. In the human lower urinary and genital tract, immunoreactivity for CB1 and CB2 has been localized in the penile erectile tissue (corpus cavernosum penis) and to nerve fibers of the urethra, and the expression of CB2 receptors, suggested to have a role in sensory (neuro)signaling, has been reported in the mucosa of the urinary bladder. The number of members of this endocannabinoid signaling system still seems to increase, as new non-CB1 and non-CB2 receptors, endocannabinoid-related molecules with little activity at the CB1 and CB2 receptors, as well as new enzymes for the biosynthesis and degradation of endocannabinoids have yet been identified. However, at the time of writing this manuscript, it still remains unclear whether compounds that can selectively interfere with the levels of endocannabinoids or their actions at CB receptors may potentially represent promising templates for new drugs to address dysfunctions of the lower urinary and also the genital tract. More conclusive evidence of the significance of molecular pathways stimulated by anandamide and other cannabinoid molecules is required. The present review aims to briefly summarize what has emerged from basic research and clinical approaches on the role of the ECS in the human LUT and in genital tissues Fig.1.
